docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Waters your garden from Home Assistant, putting back the water that sun, heat and wind took from the soil.

Smart Irrigation works out, zone by zone, how much water your plants lost to evaporation and got back from the rain, and waters the difference. No fixed fifteen minutes, no watering the day after a storm, no guessing in a heatwave. Then it runs the watering itself, as much of it as you want it to: from a duration for your own automation, to programs, schedules and pumps.

It is the official Smart Irrigation integration for Home Assistant, available by default in HACS.

docs.title: Two ways to use it
docs.text:
You choose one in Settings › General, under What Smart Irrigation does. The setup assistant asks too.

  1. Calculate only: it calculates, you water. Each zone gets a duration, a water balance and the reasons behind them, as entities and events. Your own automation, a blueprint for your controller (Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler, B-hyve, ESPHome), or Irrigation Unlimited does the watering. This is the choice of a new installation.
  2. Calculate and water: it runs your whole irrigation. Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself, with programs of ordered steps, schedules ("done by sunrise", every other day, only in summer, after another program), cycle and soak so clay takes the water in, pumps and main valves, a watchdog for a valve left open, and a planning of what will run and why. The water actually delivered is credited to each zone. It can import an Irrigation Unlimited configuration.

The third choice, Stop everything, calculates and waters nothing, for the winter.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• It measures instead of guessing. Each zone keeps a water balance in millimetres: evaporation out, rain in. When the balance says the soil is short, the zone waters exactly that much back, and not a drop more.
  • It uses the science, not a rule of thumb. Evapotranspiration comes from the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation, the reference method in agronomy, computed hour by hour or day by day, from your own sensors, a weather service, any weather integration of Home Assistant, or a mix.
  • It says why. Every calculation shows its work: what was read, what was computed, and what it decided. The Home page shows the next watering, what is watering now, and whether a run would be held back and on what numbers.
  • It does not water when it should not. Rain in the forecast, a rain sensor, frost, wind, or soil that is already wet: any of these can hold a run back, and each schedule of a program can choose which apply to it.
  • It knows a greenhouse. Under glass the sky is not what reaches the plant. A lux sensor inside answers it, and without one the glass dims the sun.
  • It is easy to start and deep when you need it. A panel built with Home Assistant's own components, in a standard mode with a setup assistant that creates your first zone, an advanced mode that opens every setting, and Edit in YAML for the few options a power user wants.
  • It fits into Home Assistant. A valve entity per zone for dashboards and voice assistants, sensors, buttons and events for your own automations, and a dashboard card that shows where each zone stands and can water one on demand.
  • It speaks your language. The panel and everything Home Assistant shows for it come in 20 languages. Most were machine-translated and wait for a native speaker: you can correct them on Weblate, in the browser.

docs.title: How it works, in one paragraph
docs.text: Water leaves the soil by evaporation and through the leaves. How fast depends on the sun, the temperature, the humidity and the wind, and that is what the FAO-56 equation computes from your weather data. Smart Irrigation adds that loss to a per-zone water balance, subtracts the rain, and when the water balance is short by more than the threshold you set, it converts the missing millimetres into a run time from the zone's own area and flow. After the run, the water balance goes back to zero and the cycle starts again. The how it works page tells it properly, and the calculation explanation on each zone shows the numbers of the day.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Home Assistant, and a way to turn your watering on and off from it.
  • Weather data, which can be your own sensors, or a weather service: Open-Meteo needs no account, OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather need a free API key.
  • A few minutes. The setup assistant asks what it needs, one question at a time, and creates the first zone for you.

Smart Irrigation opens your valves itself only if you choose Calculate and water. Otherwise it calculates, and you decide what listens.

Use this integration at your own risk

We assume no responsibility for any inconvenience caused by using it. Always use common sense before deciding to irrigate on the numbers it provides: watering during heavy rain can cause flooding.

docs.title: Manual coordinates
docs.text:
By default, Smart Irrigation reads the weather for the location set in Home Assistant. Manual coordinates (latitude, longitude and elevation) read it somewhere else, for instance when:

  • your garden is at another property than your Home Assistant;
  • you want the weather of a nearby weather station;
  • your Home Assistant location is not set precisely;
  • the elevation of your Home Assistant location is wrong or missing.

docs.title: Where
docs.text:
On the Location coordinates card, under Weather › Weather service in the Smart Irrigation panel. The card shows in advanced mode, or whenever manual coordinates are on, so coordinates in use are never out of sight.

Note

The integration's Configure button (Settings › Devices & services) does not set them. Up to 2026.11.0 it asked for coordinates, but what it saved was never used. It now only points to the panel.

docs.title: The card
docs.text:
• Use manual coordinates switches between your own coordinates and the Home Assistant location. Off, the card shows the current Home Assistant coordinates.
  • Latitude, in decimal degrees, from -90 to 90 (for example 40.7128 for New York).
  • Longitude, in decimal degrees, from -180 to 180 (for example -74.0060 for New York).
  • Elevation, in metres above sea level, from -1000 to 9000. Optional, 0 when left empty.

The values are checked as you type, up to 6 decimal places.

docs.title: How they are used
docs.text:
1. Manual coordinates, when they are on and both latitude and longitude are set.
  2. Otherwise the Home Assistant coordinates. A warning is logged if Home Assistant still has its default location.

Every weather service reads the coordinates in use:

  • Open-Meteo for the forecast, the hourly radiation history and the hourly forecast;
  • OpenWeatherMap for its calls and for the pressure at your elevation;
  • Pirate Weather for its forecasts.

They are used from the next weather update. No restart is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A garden at another property. Switch on manual coordinates, set the latitude and longitude of the garden, and its elevation if it differs much from home.

A nearby weather station. Switch on manual coordinates and enter the coordinates of the station.

A wrong elevation. Switch on manual coordinates, keep the latitude and longitude of Home Assistant, and set the correct elevation. The pressure, and so the evapotranspiration, depend on it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The coordinates do not seem to be used. Check that Use manual coordinates is on, then wait for the next weather update.

The weather data looks wrong. Check the coordinates on a map, check that the elevation is sensible, and check that the weather service's API key is valid.

The log says which coordinates are used:

INFO: Using manual coordinates: lat=40.712800, lon=-74.006000, elevation=100m
INFO: Using Home Assistant coordinates: lat=52.000000, lon=5.000000, elevation=10m

docs.title: Closed-loop watering
docs.text: With Calculate only and nothing else, Smart Irrigation runs open loop: it calculates a duration and fires an event, but it does not know whether (or how much) watering actually happened, so your automation credits the water balance. The closed-loop features remove that guesswork: Smart Irrigation credits the water balance itself, from the runs it sees or the runs it makes. Calculate and water turns them on; with Calculate only, observed watering is a switch of Settings › General on the advanced panel.

docs.title: Observed watering (credit the water balance automatically)
docs.text:
When enabled, Smart Irrigation watches each zone's linked valve/switch. Whenever it runs (a manual tap, an automation, or Smart Irrigation itself), the zone's water balance is credited from the run time and the zone's throughput (depth_mm = throughput_L_per_min x minutes / size_m2). No more manual reset.

To set it up:

  1. Choosing Calculate and water turns it on. Otherwise, on the advanced panel, switch on the Observed watering (closed loop) card of Settings › General.
  2. In Zones, set each zone's Linked valve/switch to the entity that waters that zone (a switch, valve or input_boolean).

The Smart Irrigation device has an Observed watering binary sensor (binary_sensor.smart_irrigation_observed_watering), on while the option is: one automation shared between several installs can read it to know whether it must reset the water balance itself.

Credit once

When observed watering is on, it becomes the only thing crediting the water balance. Remove any credit_watering, set_bucket or reset_bucket call from your irrigation automation, or the water is counted twice.

docs.title: Optional: leave short runs out
docs.text: A short run that only cools the plants on a hot afternoon (a few minutes to keep the leaves from wilting) mostly stays on the leaves and evaporates. Set the zone's Ignore runs up to (seconds, advanced mode) and a run of the valve that lasts that long or less is not credited, nor counted as the zone's watering of the cycle. A longer run counts in full, its first seconds included. Empty credits every run. It applies to runs Smart Irrigation observes; the runs it drives itself are credited as they always were.

docs.title: Optional: a cumulative volume meter (more precise)
docs.text:
For exact accounting you can also set a zone's Cumulative volume meter. The applied depth is then taken from the measured volume delivered during the run (meter_at_close - meter_at_open) instead of throughput x time.

It must be a cumulative water-meter total (state class total_increasing), not an instant flow rate. The unit is read automatically from the sensor (L, mL, m³, gal, ft³). An instant flow-rate sensor (for example L/min) will not work; if your hardware only exposes a rate, feed it through a Riemann-sum Integration helper first to get a cumulative total.

docs.title: Water flowing with every valve closed (advanced mode)
docs.text:
With Leak alert after set (in litres, 0 by default: not watched), a zone's meter is watched between the runs too. When it counts that much while none of the zones it measures has a valve open, nor had one open in the last three minutes (the pipe drains, a meter reports late), Smart Irrigation tells you: the hub's Leak binary sensor goes on, the event smart_irrigation_leak is fired (flow_sensor, litres, zone_ids, zones), a repair is raised and the programs' notifications are sent at once. It clears by itself once the meter has stood still for half an hour. An automation on the event or the sensor can close a main valve.

Only for a meter that measures the garden alone: a meter on the house counts the taps and the washing machine too.

docs.title: What the meter tells us about your throughput
docs.text:
Every irrigation duration is derived from the zone's configured throughput: the water balance says how many mm are missing, the size turns that into litres, and the throughput turns litres into minutes. A throughput copied off a datasheet rather than measured at the tap is one of the quietest ways to water twice as long as intended, or half as long, for a whole season.

A zone with a volume meter gives the answer for free, since a run knows both how many litres came out and how long the valve was open. Smart Irrigation divides one by the other, smooths the result over several runs, and raises a repair notice in Settings › Repairs when it drifts more than 25% from what you configured. Runs shorter than two minutes are ignored: filling the pipe dominates them.

It only ever tells you. The zone's throughput is never rewritten, because pressure varies, a meter can sit upstream of more than one zone, and silently changing how long valves stay open is not something to do behind your back. If the measurement looks right, copy it into the zone yourself.

docs.title: When Smart Irrigation runs the valves
docs.text:
With Calculate and water (see Watering with programs), Smart Irrigation opens each zone's linked valve, waits the calculated duration, then closes it. No automation of your own is needed. The water balance is credited for the runs it performs, since it knows exactly what it delivered. Observed watering, on with it, also credits any other run of that valve, which is what you want for a tap somebody opens by hand to water the same lawn. If that valve also does something else (filling a paddling pool, hosing the terrace), turn observed watering off in advanced mode.

  • The order of the zones: each program's steps decide it, a step with several zones watering them together. The Irrigate all zones button has its own order, one after the other or all at once (see Irrigate all zones now).
  • Open confirmation: before crediting, Smart Irrigation waits for the valve to report an on-state. If it never opens, the run is not credited (so the deficit stays and rolls over to the next day) and a smart_irrigation_zone_problem event is fired. A write-only valve with no readable state is given the benefit of the doubt.
  • Confirmation per zone (advanced mode): Wait for the valve to confirm (seconds), and how many times to send the open again (open_resends, YAML only, for instance open_resends: 0 in the zone's Edit in YAML). Empty keeps the defaults: 30 seconds and two resends (at 10 and 20 seconds), and 5 seconds for the valve to report a close. Set, the wait applies to the open and to the close, and the resends are spread evenly over it, so 60 seconds and 2 resends sends the open again at 20 and 40 seconds. 0 never sends it again. A cloud valve, Gardena's for instance, confirms through the vendor's servers and counts every command against a quota: give it a longer wait and 0. A close that is not confirmed is always tried a second time, whatever the resends, because a valve left open costs more than one command. This is Irrigation Unlimited's check_back (delay, retries), per zone.
  • Setting a failing zone aside (advanced mode, off by default, on the Observed watering card): with Set a zone aside after this many failed runs at 3, say, a zone whose valve did not open, gave no water or could not have its own timer set three runs in a row is no longer watered by any program or cycle, rather than failing every morning with the pump starting for nothing. You are told at once: the programs' notifications, a repair in Settings › Repairs with a button to put the zone back, the zone's problem sensor (reason zone_set_aside) and a line on the zone in the panel, with Put back. It comes back by itself when its valve is seen opening, for instance tried by hand once repaired, and a successful run counts its failures from zero again.
  • Reboot resilience: a run that is in progress when Home Assistant restarts is resumed (or closed if it already exceeded its duration) and then credited.
  • One run per zone per cycle: a zone whose valve is already open is left out, and a zone watered while it waited its turn in a sequential run is not watered again when the queue reaches it. With observed watering on, that includes a valve opened outside Smart Irrigation, by hand or by another automation: running it too would close the valve under that run and count the overlap twice.
  • One cycle at a time, in sequential mode: a run asked for while one is already going joins the queue instead of starting beside it, so two valves are never open at once. A zone already waiting is not queued twice, the zone being watered right now is not queued behind itself, and the zones that joined are in the same end-of-run summary. In parallel mode there is nothing to join: every zone at once is what that setting asks for.

Give your valve a hardware failsafe

If Home Assistant goes down for a long time during a run, the physical valve stays open and keeps watering, because Home Assistant is no longer there to close it. Give your valve a maximum run time on the device itself. Smart Irrigation also caps the credited time at the zone's maximum duration. For an MQTT or ZHA valve, Smart Irrigation can arm that failsafe for you on every run: see hardware auto-off.

docs.title: Watering one zone by hand
docs.text:
Calculate and water also adds the Irrigate now button entity of each zone and Irrigate all zones on the hub, without a reload or a restart. Leaving it makes those buttons unavailable; choosing it again restores them with the same entity ids.

With Calculate and water, each zone with a linked valve has a Water button on its card in the Zones page. It asks for minutes, and left empty it waters the run the planning shows. The valve opens straight away, or takes its turn behind what is watering, and the water is credited to the zone's balance like any run of ours. It is the smart_irrigation.water_zone action, which an automation can call with the zone's entity or its zone_id.

docs.title: Hardware auto-off (MQTT on_time dead-man)
docs.text:
The closing of the valve normally happens in Home Assistant: the run opens the valve, waits, and closes it. If Home Assistant stops in that window and never comes back, nothing sends the close and the valve keeps watering. (A restart does recover: an in-flight run is resumed and closed when Home Assistant comes back. The gap is Home Assistant staying down.)

For a valve controlled over MQTT (a zigbee2mqtt device, for instance), Smart Irrigation can close that gap with a hardware dead-man. On each pass it publishes an on with timed off command to the device, so the device's own firmware shuts the valve off after the run even if Home Assistant is no longer there. It is armed only after the valve is confirmed open, and it is additive: the normal close still runs, the on_time is set a little longer than the pass so it lands just after, as a failsafe rather than the primary off.

Three optional per-zone fields configure it (the topic and the mode on the advanced panel, shown only with Calculate and water and a linked valve set; the state key in YAML). The first two are empty by default, so nothing changes until you fill them in:

  • Safety off MQTT topic: the device's set topic, e.g. zigbee2mqtt/front_lawn_valve/set.
  • Safety off state key (safety_off_state_key, YAML only, for instance safety_off_state_key: state_l1 in the zone's Edit in YAML; empty is state): the on/off property in the payload: state for a single-channel device, or state_l1...state_l4 for one channel of a multi-channel device.
  • Safety off mode: auto (the default), zha or off, described below.

With those set, a pass that holds the valve for 300 seconds publishes {"state_l1": "ON", "on_time": 330} to the topic (the run time plus a 30-second margin). The device closes its own valve after on_time seconds whatever happens to Home Assistant.

Device support varies

on_time ("on with timed off") is honoured by the device firmware, not by Smart Irrigation, and not every device implements it. Test it before you rely on it: start a run, stop Home Assistant while the valve is open, and confirm the valve closes itself after on_time. Some devices need an off_wait_time alongside on_time to behave.

Verified

A Sonoff SWV (firmware 1.0.4) on zigbee2mqtt, topic zigbee2mqtt/<friendly name>/set, state key state: with the Zigbee coordinator unplugged in the middle of a run, the valve closed by itself at the end of it (reported in #893).

Valves on ZHA can be armed too. The linked valve must be a ZHA entity (found through the entity registry): each pass then sends the device an on with timed off command (On/Off cluster, command 0x42) through zha.issue_zigbee_cluster_command, right after the normal open (a Sonoff SWV is the exception, see below). The unit of the time differs between devices, so the safety off mode matters:

  • auto (default): armed automatically only for a model known to be verified. That is the Sonoff SWV (manufacturer SONOFF, model SWV), tested on a real valve (firmware 1.0.04, ZHA): it honours the command, but counts the time in seconds, not in tenths of a second as the ZCL spec says. Smart Irrigation sends it the pass length plus the margin, in seconds (at most 65535 s, about 18 hours). If Home Assistant dies mid-run, the valve closes itself about 30 seconds after the time Home Assistant would have closed it. If a topic is set, the topic wins and ZHA is not used.
  • zha: explicit opt-in, arms any ZHA valve. A model that is not known is sent the time in the ZCL unit (tenths of a second); a pass longer than 6553 s is then not armed (a warning is logged once), as the device would close the valve too early. Other models are unverified: test them before you rely on them.
  • off: never armed.

A Sonoff SWV is opened by that same command. On a real valve, on with timed off sent to a closed SWV both opens it and starts its own timer, so there is no moment when it is open without a timer. For a SWV in auto mode (no MQTT topic, mode auto; in zha or off mode the normal open is used), Smart Irrigation therefore opens the linked valve with that single command instead of the normal open: the time is the pass length rounded up plus the 30-second margin, in seconds (at most 65535). The rest is unchanged: the open is confirmed the same way (an open that has to be repeated sends the same command), the close at the normal time also clears the device's timer, a cycle-and-soak pass opens again and so restarts the timer, and a run resumed after a restart opens the same way with the time that remains. The extra valves keep the normal open. Each attempt is short (6 seconds, because a battery valve is asleep most of the time and would otherwise hold the start for about 16 seconds), and the command is tried once. If it fails (ZHA not set up, an error, a valve that does not answer), a warning is logged once for the zone and the valve is opened the normal way, followed by the separate arm described above: the watering is never prevented. Any other valve (another ZHA model, the explicit zha mode on an unknown model, MQTT, other platforms) is opened and armed exactly as before.

This timed off is separate from, and different from, the valve's own water shortage auto close, which does not cover Home Assistant stopping in the middle of a run. A failure to send the command never breaks the run: it is logged as a warning the first time for a zone, then at debug level.

The per-zone safety off mode picks the behaviour: auto (the default) uses the MQTT topic if there is one, else arms a Sonoff SWV on ZHA, and otherwise nothing; zha also arms a ZHA valve when there is no topic; off never arms a dead-man for that zone, topic included. Only the zone's linked valve is armed, not its extra valves.

A valve that closes after a duration of its own is opened for that duration, not until it is told to close. A Gardena smart valve is one: the Gardena integration opens it for its watering duration number, one minute unless changed, so a 40-minute pass would water for one minute while Smart Irrigation counts it as open. For such a valve, set the zone's Valve's own duration (advanced panel, with Calculate and water and a linked valve set) to that number entity, or to an input_number your valve reads. Before each open Smart Irrigation writes the pass length plus the 30-second margin to it, in the entity's unit (s, min or h), rounded up to its step: a 40-minute pass sets a minutes number to 41. The valve then stays open for the whole pass, Smart Irrigation closes it at the normal time, and the valve's own timer is the dead-man. A pass longer than the entity's maximum gets the maximum, and a warning is logged once: the valve will then close before the pass ends. A missing entity, one whose unit is not a duration, or a failed write is logged and the valve opens with whatever duration it already has. The safety off mode off turns it off as well.

Only water with the valve's own timer. Setting the valve's own timer is best-effort: when it fails (a battery valve asleep, MQTT down, a duration that could not be written), the valve opens all the same, without that safety net for the run. A zone that would rather skip the watering can say so: If the valve's own timer can't be set (advanced panel, shown only for a zone whose valve has a timer Smart Irrigation can set: a ZHA valve, an MQTT topic or a valve's own duration) set to Leave the valve shut. The valve then stays shut, or is shut at once when the timer is armed right after the open (MQTT, or a ZHA valve other than a Sonoff SWV), nothing is credited, so the water is carried over to the next watering, and the zone reports valve_timer_not_set. A zone with that setting and no way of setting a timer at all is never opened. Home Assistant still closes the valve at the normal time either way: the valve's own timer is the second net, not a replacement.

Other valves (Wi-Fi switches, ESPHome, Tuya, or anything that is neither MQTT with a topic nor ZHA) get no automatic dead-man: leave the fields empty and the run behaves exactly as before. For those, set the failsafe on the device itself, which is more reliable than Home Assistant sending it every run: a Shelly has an Auto-off timer, Tasmota has PulseTime, ESPHome can turn a switch off after a delay, and many Tuya Wi-Fi switches have a countdown function.

docs.title: Cycle and soak, and the pause between zones
docs.text:
Both are for an installation that is already tuned, and only apply when Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself (Calculate and water). Each step of a program has its own number of passes, and the soak time between them is one setting for every program, shown next to a step's passes. The order, passes and pause of the Irrigate all zones button are folded at the bottom of Watering › Programs.

Water in several passes splits a run into shorter passes with a pause between them. Clay and compacted soil have an infiltration rate: past it the water runs off or puddles, and the zone is billed for water the roots never see. Three passes of five minutes with fifteen minutes of soaking deliver the same water as one run of fifteen minutes, and the soil keeps more of it. Guidance: sand takes water as fast as you can give it, so leave this at one pass; loam rarely needs more than two; clay and slopes are what it is for.

The plan is fixed when the run starts, and a run too short to split is left alone (no pass shorter than a minute). Each pass is credited as it closes, so a restart in the middle of a run never credits water twice and never leaves a valve open.

Pause between zones waits between two zones of a sequential run, for the line pressure to recover or for a slow valve to finish closing before the next one opens.

Both lengthen the run without adding water to it, and a schedule that must be done by sunrise works back from the whole thing, soaking and pauses included: three zones of half an hour in three passes with fifteen minutes of soaking occupy two and a half hours, not an hour and a half. Watch that against the hour you want to be finished by. With Calculate only, your own executor opens the valves, neither setting applies, and the start trigger works back from the watering alone.

docs.title: Events for your own automations
docs.text:
When Smart Irrigation waters, it fires events you can use to notify or react, so you do not need one automation per zone. With Calculate and water, the first two come from the run of the Irrigate all zones button, and from the program with the id main (on an installation that had a main program, the ordinary program it was turned into, Watering; there is no main program any more), so an automation written for them keeps working; every program also fires smart_irrigation_program_started and smart_irrigation_program_finished.

  • smart_irrigation_irrigation_started when a run begins. Data: sequencing (sequential/parallel) and zones, a list of {zone_id, zone, seconds} about to be watered.
  • smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished when the whole run is done. Data: zones, a list of {zone_id, zone, seconds, volume_l, bucket} that ran (volume delivered and the new water balance), and problems, a list of {zone_id, zone, reason} for zones that delivered no water: the valve did not open (valve_did_not_open), or it opened and the zone's flow meter did not move (no_flow). A valve that watered but would not close is still in zones, since the water it delivered is credited, and is reported by its own smart_irrigation_zone_problem event.
  • smart_irrigation_zone_problem the moment something goes wrong with a valve. Data: zone_id, zone, entity_id, reason: valve_did_not_open, valve_did_not_close (the close failed or the valve still reads open, retried once), or no_flow (the valve opened but the zone's flow meter did not move, so the run is not credited), valve_closed_early (the valve read off or closed while it should have been open, so the zone's run ends and is credited for the time it was open), supply_did_not_turn_on (the pump or main valve the zone depends on never came on, so the zone's valve stays shut), or valve_timer_not_set (the zone asks for the valve's own timer and it could not be set, so the valve stays shut or is shut at once).

Example: a single end-of-watering report for all zones.

alias: Watering report
triggers:
  - trigger: event
    event_type: smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished
actions:
  - variables:
      zones: "{{ trigger.event.data.zones }}"
      problems: "{{ trigger.event.data.problems }}"
  - action: notify.mobile_app_your_phone
    data:
      title: "Watering finished{{ ' with problems' if problems | count > 0 else '' }}"
      message: >-
        {% set l = namespace(t=[]) %}
        {% for z in zones %}
          {% set l.t = l.t + [z.zone ~ ": " ~ (z.seconds / 60) | round(1) ~ " min, " ~ z.volume_l ~ " L"] %}
        {% endfor %}
        {% for p in problems %}
          {% set l.t = l.t + ["WARNING " ~ p.zone ~ ": " ~ p.reason] %}
        {% endfor %}
        {{ l.t | join("\n") }}
mode: single

Remove your old watering automations

If you had one automation per zone that opened the valve and called set_bucket or reset_bucket, remove them once you choose Calculate and water: Smart Irrigation opens the valves and credits the water balance itself, so the old automations would double up. Keep only report or notification automations like the one above.

With Calculate only, Smart Irrigation opens no valve: it fires smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones at the start trigger for your own automation or executor, with the trigger's identity. See events.

docs.title: General settings
docs.text:
Settings › General holds the settings of the whole installation. The first card says what Smart Irrigation does; the others come in three sections:

  • Calculation: when the durations are worked out and how, the seasonal adjustments and the calculation log.
  • Control: with Calculate only, the start triggers; on the advanced panel, observed watering.
  • System: Advanced settings, the blueprints, the setup assistant and the import from Irrigation Unlimited.

The weather service, the location, how often the weather is read, and the checks that skip a run (the days between irrigation included) are on the Weather tab: see Weather configuration.

docs.title: Calculate and water, calculate only, or stop everything
docs.text:
The first card, Smart Irrigation, has one list, What Smart Irrigation does:

  • Calculate and water: Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself, with its programs: steps, schedules, pumps and main valves, and a Watering tab in the panel.
  • Calculate only, the choice of a new installation: Smart Irrigation works out the water balances and the durations and fires its start event at the start trigger. An automation of your own, Irrigation Unlimited or your controller does the watering with those durations. Smart Irrigation opens no valve. A watering by hand can still be credited with observed watering.
  • Stop everything, described below.

Leaving Calculate and water stops what Smart Irrigation is watering at once.

Coming from 2026.11.0 or earlier

This one list replaced the master switch, the Full controller switch and Let Smart Irrigation control the valve. An installation was moved over once, keeping its watering as it was: see Watering with programs.

docs.title: Stop everything
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation:

  • keeps taking its weather readings and keeps its sensors up to date;
  • calculates nothing, and leaves every zone's water balance as it is;
  • opens no valve and runs no program. After a restart, a run that was interrupted is closed rather than resumed;
  • fires no start event: a start trigger that is reached fires smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped with the reason irrigation_off (see events).

When it calculates again, the time it was stopped is not counted: each zone's next calculation starts at that moment, as after setting a water balance by hand, so the first run is not weeks of evaporation at once.

The hub device's switch Calculate and water (switch.smart_irrigation_irrigation_enabled) is off while everything is stopped, for an automation or a dashboard (the end of the season, for instance). It stays on with Calculate only.

Stopping is not the same as postponing: a postponement holds the automatic watering back for a while and keeps calculating, so the zones are owed what the weather took meanwhile.

docs.title: Calculating the watering duration
docs.text:
One choice, Watering duration calculated, says when the durations are worked out:

  • At a fixed time. Every day at Calculate at (23:00 unless you change it), the water lost is added to each zone's water balance and the durations are set. Use it when something other than Smart Irrigation starts the watering and reads the durations whenever it likes (Irrigation Unlimited, or a schedule of your own).
  • Just before each start. The zones are calculated again when a program or the start trigger begins, with the freshest weather. There is no time to choose. Use it when Smart Irrigation itself starts the watering (Calculate and water, or the start event of Calculate only). With no evening calculation to set the durations, the start is placed from the live estimate of the run's length, and placed again at every weather reading. See Just before each start.
  • Only when I ask. Nothing is calculated by itself. Use the calculate buttons or the services.

What starts the watering is decided elsewhere: the programs' schedules with Calculate and water, the start trigger with Calculate only. Calculate evapotranspiration hour by hour, under the choice, changes the form of the equation, not the moment of the calculation.

How the choice maps to the old settings

The stored settings are unchanged: At a fixed time is the old "automatically calculate" setting being on, Just before each start is the old "calculate again before the first start" setting being on, and Only when I ask is both being off.

What a calculation reads. Each zone reads only the weather readings that arrived since its own last calculation, and remembers how far it has read. Readings are dropped once every zone using that sensor group has consumed them, so two zones sharing a group can calculate at different times without either of them losing data. Readings are also capped at a week, so nothing piles up even if a zone stops calculating.

Rain between the calculation and the start. Watering usually starts hours after the calculation, and it can rain in between. At the start, each automatic zone's duration is worked out again against the rain collected since its calculation, so a night of rain shortens the run or cancels it.

The water balance itself is left alone by that. It is a running balance: watering credits it with the water actually applied, and the next calculation adds the whole interval's rain, so crediting the rain at the start as well would count it twice. A run is only ever shortened this way, never lengthened, and a dry night leaves the calculated duration as it is.

The run still starts at the time it was scheduled for. A start that must be done by sunrise works back from the duration known at calculation time, so a run shortened by rain finishes early rather than starting late.

docs.title: Calculate evapotranspiration hour by hour
docs.text:
On for a new installation, off for one that already existed. A fresh installation starts on it, because it is the better arithmetic. An installation set up before it arrived keeps the daily equation until its owner switches, because the two give different numbers and nobody's watering should change on an update without being asked.

When on, Smart Irrigation sums the FAO-56 hourly equation (Eq. 53) over each hour of the zone's window instead of running the daily equation on the window's averages. The daily form is biased by cloudiness, because an average day hides whether the sun and the heat came together; summing the hours removes most of that bias.

Calculating hour by hour at all is an idea taken from JustChr's Irrigation Plus fork, which is where it was first tried on this integration; the equations here are written from FAO-56 itself and checked against the paper's own worked example.

It needs temperature, humidity and wind speed in the sensor group (a sensor or a weather service), and the site's coordinates.

It is worth having when readings arrive through the day. Each hour is priced from the readings of that hour, so an update interval of minutes or an hour is what the form is for.

One update a day leaves a single reading held across twenty-four hours: it still runs, and it does not produce nonsense, but the hours then differ only by the sun and the result is no more trustworthy than the daily equation's on the same data. Measured on a synthetic clear day, which of the two lands closer to the truth in that case depends on the hour the samples fell in. If your sensor group updates once or twice a day, raise the update frequency before reading anything into either form.

Solar radiation without a sensor. The hourly equation needs the sun of each hour, and there are three ways it can have it. A group with a radiation or illuminance sensor reads its own, as before. A group without one whose weather service can be asked reads the service's own hourly history, which measures and models it: Open-Meteo publishes it, and OpenWeatherMap or Pirate Weather answer through the Open-Meteo fallback they already use for radiation.

An installation with neither, a set of plain sensors and no weather service, estimates it: the day's temperature range gives the day's radiation (FAO-56 Eq. 50, the same equation the daily form falls back on), and the sun's own path over that day says which hours received it. Summed over a day the estimate is exactly what the daily equation would have used, so the amount of sun credited does not change; what changes is that it is placed on the hours it belongs to, which is the bias the hourly form exists to remove. The calculation log records whether the sun of a run was measured or estimated.

A greenhouse is the exception and keeps the daily equation when it has no sensor of its own: no reading of the sky describes what reaches a plant under glass, so there is nothing to estimate from. A lux sensor on the inside answers that properly, and the sensor group takes one.

A group fed by Open-Meteo is priced on Open-Meteo's own hours. Smart Irrigation reads the weather service about once an hour, and each reading stands in for the hour around it; Open-Meteo's own hourly figures are means over the hour, and they differ when the sun moves fast, in the morning and in the evening. For a sensor group whose every source is the weather service, and a weather service that is Open-Meteo, the hourly equation is therefore fed the hours Open-Meteo publishes for the window (temperature, humidity, wind and pressure at the ends of each hour, and the radiation of the hour itself) instead of the readings Smart Irrigation took.

On a real autumn day this brought the result from 8% below Open-Meteo's own evapotranspiration to about 3% below it. A group that measures some inputs and reads the others from Open-Meteo gets both: Open-Meteo's own hours for the inputs it reads from the service, and its sensors or static values for the ones it measures, hour by hour. An hour Open-Meteo has not published yet keeps the readings. Another weather service or a greenhouse keeps summing its own readings, and so does any group when the history cannot be read.

Nights, and why the result can read a few percent under Open-Meteo. The hourly equation (FAO-56, Eq. 53) is built for the hours with sun, and the night is where it is least certain. A night hour has no radiation to measure, so the sky has to be assumed to know how much heat the ground loses, and a night's wind and dry air can add as much as they like. Two things are worth knowing:

  • Which sky. FAO-56 gives two ways. The preferred one carries the ratio of measured to clear-sky radiation from the daylight into the night, and that is what a calculation does whenever its window contains daylight. The other, which the paper calls "more approximate", assumes a ratio of 0.4 to 0.6 at night in humid climates and 0.7 to 0.8 in arid ones; Smart Irrigation reads it off the humidity of the hour, and uses it only when the window has no daylight to measure from (the live estimate in the small hours, a calculation over a few hours of night). Open-Meteo uses that second way for every night. On clear windy autumn days the first way loses more heat at night, so Smart Irrigation reads 5 to 10% under Open-Meteo's own evapotranspiration, almost all of it from the night hours, while the daylight hours agree to within a few percent. Both are FAO-56; neither is measured against the ground here.
  • Nothing is negative. A calm humid night prices a hair below zero, which is dew forming on the leaves and not water in the soil. Every hour is worth zero at the least, and a window's total never falls as the window grows, so a water balance never rises without rain. Open-Meteo reports 0.00 for those hours too.

The American standard of the same equation (ASCE-EWRI 2005) goes further than FAO-56 at night, with a larger surface-resistance term (Cd of 0.96 against 0.24 by day, for the short reference). That would lower the night hours, not raise them. Smart Irrigation keeps FAO-56's single form, whose worked example is its test, and reports the difference rather than tune the model to another implementation.

Forecast days. A zone whose module looks ahead waters on the mean of today and the days to come, so a hot tomorrow raises today's run. Those days are now read hour by hour as well: each one is priced as its own 24 hours, and the measured window joins the average as the rate per day it implies. Every term of that mean is then hourly, which is the point, since averaging an hourly sum with a day computed from its own averages would put the bias straight back in.

With any other module, or when the hours cannot be reconstructed (no readings, a field missing everywhere, a greenhouse with no radiation or illuminance sensor, or fewer forecast days available than the module asks for), the daily equation keeps being used, so switching it on never leaves a zone without a calculation. The calculation explanation says which form was used.

docs.title: Just before each start
docs.text:
The calculation at a fixed time prices the evapotranspiration, the temperature and the wind of the hours before it. A start at sunset then waters on data some twenty hours old; only the rain was brought up to date at the start (rain since the calculation, the forecast, the rain history).

With Just before each start, the zones are calculated again, with fresh weather, when the watering starts. It happens before every start, not only the first of the day: a second run on a hot afternoon waters for what the zones lost since the morning's run. Nothing is done when a zone was calculated within the hour, and a calculation that fails leaves the run to go ahead on the earlier numbers.

docs.title: Count only rain that reaches the roots
docs.text:
A switch of the Calculating the watering duration card, on for a new installation. An installation that already existed keeps its setting as it was.

Advanced mode

The switch is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode while it is off.

A shower smaller than a fifth of the evapotranspiration of the period wets the leaves and evaporates before the soil sees it, so it is not counted as water for the roots. It acts on the rain that fell, in every calculation, and has nothing to do with the rain forecast of the Skip watering page.

It is judged on the whole period between two calculations, not day by day, so a period of several days ignores less than a day-by-day reading would. It does not model runoff on heavy rain; the maximum water balance still caps what the soil keeps.

docs.title: Seasonal adjustments
docs.text:
Advanced mode

The Seasonal adjustments card is on the advanced panel.

An adjustment covers a range of months (November to February is a range, and so is March to September) and some zones (all, or their numbers separated by commas). It does two things:

  • its crop factor multiplier scales the crop factor of those zones for those months (1 changes nothing, 0.5 halves the water use);
  • its threshold offset is added to their irrigation threshold.

Several adjustments that cover the same month multiply. They apply to the evapotranspiration, not to the duration, so the water balance follows the season.

The same adjustments can be made from automations with the set_seasonal_adjustment action. For a crop with a crop factor for every month, the zone's Crop factor by month table is easier than twelve adjustments.

docs.title: Calculation log
docs.text:
Two days with what looks like nearly identical weather can water very differently, and once a calculation has run there is normally no way to see why. The Calculation log switch, on the Calculating the watering duration card, appends one record per zone calculation to config/smart_irrigation/calc_log.jsonl (one JSON object per line, in metric units), so days can be compared afterwards instead of reconstructed by hand.

Advanced mode

The switch is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode once it is on.

Each record holds the complete chain:

  • Identification: local and UTC timestamp, zone, sensor group, calculation module, integration version.
  • Inputs: the interval used (start, end, hours) and, per field, the aggregated value, the aggregation applied (average, sum, minimum, maximum, Riemann sum, delta...), how many records went into it, their minimum and maximum, the source (sensor, weather service, static) and whether the value was carried over from the last entry.
  • Module intermediates: for the FAO-56 calculation (PyETO) the latitude, elevation, coastal flag, day of year, et_rad, cs_rad, sol_rad (and whether it was provided or estimated from temperature), net_in_sol_rad, avp, net_out_lw_rad, net_rad and eto, per day, plus the deltas list and its mean. The Passthrough and Static modules record their (fewer) inputs the same way.
  • Outputs: ET deficiency, interval multiplier, precipitation, delta, water balance before and after, maximum water balance, drainage rate and drainage, precipitation rate, resulting duration and the volume in m³.

Dry runs (the dry_run option of the calculate service) are logged too, since they are exactly when you ask "why this number?". Every record carries a dry_run flag, so a dry run is never mistaken for a real calculation.

The log is off by default. The file is capped at 2 MB and rotated (one backup kept), so it can stay on for a whole season. The most recent records are also included in the diagnostics download, with coordinates rounded and entity ids removed, so they can be attached to an issue in one step.

To compare two days, for example with jq:

jq -c 'select(.zone.name == "Lawn") | {t: .timestamp, eto: .module.days[0].eto, sol_rad: .module.days[0].sol_rad, estimated: .module.days[0].sol_rad_estimated, bucket: .outputs.bucket_after, duration: .outputs.duration}' calc_log.jsonl
Automatic weather data pruning (removed)

Weather data used to be cleared on a timer, and that setting no longer does anything. Pruning after each calculation now keeps the collected data from growing without end. The timer also threw away readings nobody had consumed: it ran at a fixed time while the calculation time is yours to choose, so moving the calculation earlier silently lost everything collected between the two, every night. A calculation at 18:55 against the default clear at 23:59 discarded five hours of evaporation a day.

The Clear all weather data action, under Zones, is still there for a deliberate reset.

docs.title: Start triggers
docs.text:
With Calculate only, the Start triggers card says when Smart Irrigation fires its start event, smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones, which your automation, blueprint or controller listens to (see events). With Calculate and water the card is not shown: each program's schedules start it.

Active trigger picks the one trigger that starts the watering, once a day:

  • Default: done by sunrise. It starts early enough that watering finishes at sunrise: sunrise minus the planned length of the run. With zone sequencing one zone at a time, that length is the sum of the zones' durations; all zones at once, the longest of them.
  • A trigger you added with Add trigger: sunrise, sunset, a solar azimuth or a fixed time, moved by Before (-) or after (+), in minutes. A fixed time suits watering that has to be done by a certain hour whatever the season. With Account for duration on, the trigger works back from its moment so watering finishes then; off, watering starts then. That applies to a fixed time as well: 06:30 with it on and an hour-long run starts at 05:30.
  • None. Nothing starts the watering, whatever the weather, while the durations are still calculated. The Info page then says "No trigger is active".

The skip conditions still apply: when they hold a start back, no start event is fired, and smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped is fired instead.

docs.title: Observed watering
docs.text:
Advanced mode

The Observed watering (closed loop) card is on the advanced panel. Choosing Calculate and water turns observed watering on by itself.

Its switch credits the water balance with what really ran: see observed watering. The card also holds:

  • Leak alert after, with observed watering on: see water flowing with every valve closed;
  • with Calculate and water, Set a zone aside after this many failed runs: see when Smart Irrigation runs the valves;
  • with Calculate only, Zone sequencing: whether the start trigger works back from the sum of the durations (one zone at a time) or from the longest one (all zones at once).

With Calculate and water, the order of the zones is set by each program's steps, and the order, passes and pause of the Irrigate all zones button are under Watering › Programs (see Irrigate all zones now).

docs.title: Advanced settings and the setup assistant
docs.text: The first card of System has the Advanced settings switch, which shows the extra settings these pages mark as "advanced mode" (see Standard and advanced). The setup assistant and the import from Irrigation Unlimited are the next cards.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation copies its example blueprints into your blueprints/ folder when it starts, each one once: a blueprint you delete is not put back. Switch off Blueprints (install the example blueprints) to copy none at all. The ones already in the folder are left as they are; delete them by hand if you do not want them.

Advanced mode

The switch is on the advanced panel, beside Advanced settings, and shows in every mode once it is off.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: The panel and the configuration flow are available in 20 languages. Most were machine-translated: you can correct them. The French is written with "tu".

docs.title: Unit system
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation follows the unit system of Home Assistant (metric or imperial). When you change it:

  • the sensor entities show their values in the new units at once;
  • the panel shows its measurements in the new units;
  • stored settings, such as thresholds, keep their values and are shown in the new units;
  • no restart or reload is needed.

Everything is stored in metric and converted only where it is shown or entered.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module is the method used to work out how much water evaporated.

You no longer create or pick one. A zone says how it is calculated, in plain words, in its Evapotranspiration field: Calculated by Smart Irrigation, Provided by a sensor or a service, or A fixed amount. The module behind that answer is created and reused for you, one per zone, and its own settings (how many days to look ahead, coastal, the fixed amount) are on the zone card too. There is no modules page any more: the three modes below are what those three answers mean.

The sensor group still records which kind of module it feeds, because what sources a group has to provide depends on it. When one group feeds zones that are calculated differently, it records none and each zone answers for itself.

docs.title: The three modes
docs.text:
They differ in one thing: where the evapotranspiration figure comes from. Everything after that (the water balance, the rain, the duration) is the same whichever you choose.

The zone's answer Mode Where the figure comes from What you need A fixed amount Manual You give one number, used every day Nothing Provided by a sensor or a service Standard An evapotranspiration figure that already exists A weather service that publishes one, or your own sensor Calculated by Smart Irrigation Advanced Computed from the weather, with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith Temperature, humidity, pressure and wind, ideally solar radiation

If you are unsure, Provided by a sensor or a service with Open-Meteo is the shortest path to something correct: it is free, needs no API key, and publishes a reference evapotranspiration computed the same way Smart Irrigation would.

Names in the code

The setup assistant's summary uses the mode names (Manual, Standard, Advanced). In the logs, the services and the stored configuration, the modules are still called Static, Passthrough and PyETO.

docs.title: A fixed amount (Manual)
docs.text:
A fixed amount of evaporation per day, which you set on the zone card (Evaporation per day), as a positive number: 4 means the zone loses 4 mm a day. No sensors and no weather service.

It is coarser than the other two, but it is not the same as no integration at all: rain still counts against it, the water balance still tracks what you have already applied, and the duration still follows from your zone's size and throughput. Somewhere around 4 to 5 mm a day is a common starting point for a temperate summer, and worth adjusting by season.

Coming from v2026.10.6 or earlier

Underneath, the module stores the amount as the change to the water balance, -4. A positive value stored before v2026.10.7 added water every day instead, and is turned around when Smart Irrigation starts.

docs.title: Provided by a sensor or a service (Standard)
docs.text:
Takes an evapotranspiration figure that already exists and uses it as it stands.

Two ways to feed it: a weather service that publishes one, which among the online services means Open-Meteo, or a sensor of your own that reports evapotranspiration. Set the Evapotranspiration source of the sensor group accordingly (Ready-made ET₀ from the weather service, or the sensor).

Rain still counts: the water balance is the evapotranspiration from this figure minus the precipitation your sensor group reports. Nothing else is required, and the group does not ask for temperature or wind, because this mode never reads them.

docs.title: Calculated by Smart Irrigation (Advanced)
docs.text:
The full FAO-56 Penman-Monteith calculation, from the individual weather quantities. The most accurate option when your sensors sit where the plants are, and the one that asks for the most.

It reads temperature, dew point, humidity, pressure, wind speed and solar radiation from the sensor group. Solar radiation is the term that drives the result: when a source provides it, it is used; when none does, it is estimated from the daily temperature range, which is coarser but still workable. Under glass, a light sensor can stand in for a radiation sensor, described under sensor groups.

Two settings of its own, on the zone:

  • Coastal site (advanced mode): for a location on or near the coast of a large land mass, or anywhere air masses are influenced by a nearby body of water. It adjusts the radiation estimate.
  • Look ahead (advanced mode): how many forecast days to fold into the calculation. 0 uses today's weather only; a higher value averages today's evapotranspiration with the forecast evapotranspiration of that many days to come, so a hot tomorrow raises today's run. It never reads forecast rain: a cloudy, humid day ahead only lowers the average a little, whatever rain is forecast. To hold a run back ahead of rain, use the rain forecast check under Skipping a run. It needs a weather service.

docs.title: Adding and deleting a module
docs.text: A zone creates the module behind it when you choose how it is calculated, and a module nothing uses any more is removed. The setup assistant creates the module, the sensor group and the zone together, from your answers.

docs.title: Sensor groups
docs.text:
A sensor group says where the weather data of its zones comes from, value by value. Any numeric Home Assistant sensor can be a source, whatever its origin. If a weather service is on, it can supply values too, and a static value can stand in for one you do not measure.

The sensor groups are under Weather › Sensor groups.

docs.title: Continuous updates
docs.text:
The Continuous updates for all sensor groups card sits above the sensor groups and applies to every group.

Advanced mode

The card is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode once it is on. Its Sensor debounce (100 ms by default) shows in every mode once it is changed.

Continuous updates records every change of a sensor of the group, instead of one reading per update, so the averages the calculation works from, hour by hour and for the rain, follow the day more finely. Every sensor group with sensors of its own is recorded this way, also one that takes the rest of its data from a weather service: its sensors are recorded as they change, and the service is still read once per update, so it costs no extra requests.

A rain gauge gains the most from it: the replay of the rain places what falls between two of its reports, so a gauge that reports every ten minutes places its rain within ten minutes rather than within the hour of the update.

It records and nothing more. The zones are calculated at the scheduled time, once, from the readings recorded, like any other zone. The live estimate on the Info page and the zone's Live water balance entity show where a zone stands in between, without writing anything. The debounce sets how fast changes are recorded.

With it on, a group's readings are combined differently: see the column Aggregation with continuous updates below.

Coming from an older version

Continuous updates used to calculate the zones again at every change, which moved the water balance, and the start that accounts for the duration of the run, all day.

docs.title: Adding a sensor group
docs.text: Select Add sensor group below the groups, enter a name and add it; with no group yet, the field is already open. Then choose the source of each value.

docs.title: Configuring a sensor group
docs.text:
Each value can come from a weather service (once one is on), a sensor, or a static value. With a sensor or a static value, make sure the unit Smart Irrigation expects is the one your sensor gives. Use your own sensors as much as you can, and the weather service for the rest.

The group's Evapotranspiration source is always the first field, and it decides what else is asked. Left on None, the zones calculate evapotranspiration from the weather, so the readings it needs are asked: temperature, dew point, humidity, pressure, wind speed and solar radiation. Given ready-made, by a weather service or a sensor, the other readings are not asked (a note says how many); rain stays. A plain sentence under each source explains what it does.

The two choices are worded to tell them apart: None (Smart Irrigation calculates it) means the weather service, or your sensors, only supply the inputs of Smart Irrigation's own calculation, and Ready-made ET₀ from the weather service (or a sensor) means the value is taken as it comes and the other readings are not used.

The group also says when its zones and its source disagree: a zone calculated from the weather ignores a provided value, and a zone set to provided needs a source.

Some fields are only shown in advanced mode:

  • Total precipitation (a rain gauge that adds up), unless it already has a source;
  • How the readings are combined (average, first, last, maximum, median, minimum, Riemann sum, sum, delta).

The question Input provides values in is only asked when Home Assistant reports no unit the field can be read in, or when the stored unit contradicts what it reports.

The following data can be provided:

Data Required Sources Units Aggregation Aggregation with continuous updates Current precipitation No Weather service, sensor, static value mm/h, in/h Average Riemann sum Dew point Yes Weather service, sensor, static value °C, °F Average Last Evapotranspiration No None (Smart Irrigation calculates it), ready-made ET₀ from the weather service, sensor, static value mm, in Average Last Humidity Yes Weather service, sensor, static value % Average Last Total precipitation No Sensor, static value mm, in Delta Delta Pressure Yes Weather service, sensor, static value hPa, millibar, inch Hg, psi Average Last Solar radiation No Weather service (or none: estimated), radiation sensor, light sensor (lux), static value W/m², MJ/day/m², W/sq ft, MJ/day/sq ft Average Riemann sum Temperature Yes Weather service, sensor, static value °C, °F Average Last Wind speed Yes Weather service, sensor, static value km/h, m/s, mph, knot Average Last

With continuous updates, every aggregation is expected to be Last, except solar radiation and current precipitation (Riemann sum) and total precipitation (Delta).

docs.title: Pressure and humidity
docs.text:
• Pressure can be absolute or relative. Absolute is the pressure measured at your location; relative is the pressure brought to sea level. Check which one your source gives.
  • Humidity is the humidity of the air, not of the soil. A soil moisture sensor gives no useful reading here; give it to the zone instead (see soil moisture).

docs.title: Wind speed at 2 m
docs.text:
The calculation uses the wind at 2 m. A weather service's wind is converted for you. For a wind sensor, the Anemometer height field takes the height in metres your anemometer is mounted at, and the reading is brought down to 2 m with the FAO-56 wind profile (equation 47). Leave it empty if the sensor is already at 2 m; a height of 2 m, or of 0.5 m or less, leaves the reading as it is. Sensor groups made before this field existed are left as they were.

Advanced mode

Anemometer height is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode once it is set.

Instead of the field, you can make a template sensor return the wind at 2 m yourself:

template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Wind speed at 2 m
        state: >-
          {{ states('sensor.your_wind_speed') | float(0) * (4.87 / log(67.8 * 10 - 5.42)) }}

Replace sensor.your_wind_speed with your sensor, and 10 with the height of the anemometer in metres. The result is in the unit of your sensor.

docs.title: Rain
docs.text:
Current precipitation is a rate (mm/h or in/h), and total precipitation a depth (mm or in) over the interval. Only one of them feeds the water balance: total precipitation when it has a value, current precipitation only when it does not. A rain rate sensor is never counted on top of a rain gauge.

  • Total precipitation is for a rain gauge of your own that adds up, which is more accurate than any service. Use the Delta aggregation with a sensor that accumulates over a period ("daily rain", "weekly rain", "total rain"): it handles resets, such as a daily total going back to zero at midnight. It takes precedence over the service's rate, so the two are never added together.
  • Current precipitation with Average uses the mean rate over the interval, which is right for evenly spaced samples; with Riemann sum the samples are integrated over their own timestamps, which is more accurate when they are not evenly spaced.

A weather service supplies the rain that fell, not the daily total. A service's daily precipitation figure is a forecast for the part of the day that has not happened yet, so crediting it would add rain that may never fall. With a weather service, leave total precipitation unset and take current precipitation from the service. How the rain is measured depends on the service:

  • Open-Meteo keeps an hourly precipitation history. At every calculation the rain of each full hour since the last calculation is read from it and credited, so every hour counts once, however often weather data is collected. If the history cannot be read, the sampled rate is used, as for the other services.
  • OpenWeatherMap reports the rain of the last hour and Pirate Weather the rate at this instant. That rate is collected at every update and integrated over the interval since the last calculation.

With OpenWeatherMap or Pirate Weather, set the automatic update interval to 1 hour or shorter. These services report the last hour only, so collecting every few hours leaves the hours in between unobserved, and rain falling in them is not counted. Only the hours actually observed are credited, so a coarse interval under-reports rain rather than scaling up what it happened to see. A warning is logged if the interval is longer than an hour. Open-Meteo's rain does not depend on the update interval.

A weather entity of Home Assistant reports no rain that fell: give the group a rain sensor.

docs.title: Greenhouse
docs.text:
A sensor group has a Greenhouse switch, for anything under glass or plastic: a greenhouse, a polytunnel. Turning it on takes precipitation out of the water balance for every zone of that group and hides its rain fields, because rain measured outside waters nothing inside.

A rain forecast is a statement about the sky. When it would skip a run, the zones of a greenhouse group go ahead and only the zones the rain can reach are held back. Their deficit is untouched and rolls over to the next run. If nothing in your installation is under glass, the run is skipped as before.

Two things the switch does not decide for you:

  • give Wind speed a static value near 0, because the FAO-56 aerodynamic term assumes open air;
  • give Solar radiation a light sensor, as below.

A light sensor can stand in for a solar radiation sensor. Under glass there is no usable sky, so a weather service has nothing relevant to say, and the calculation loses the term that drives it. Most greenhouses have no pyranometer, but a light sensor is cheap and common. Set the source of solar radiation to Light sensor (lux), pick your illuminance entity, and the reading is converted to W/m² and fed to the same Penman-Monteith calculation a real radiation sensor would feed.

The conversion divides lux by the luminous efficacy of daylight, and that efficacy depends on the sky: roughly 112 lm/W under a clear sky and up to 125 or more under an overcast one. Smart Irrigation uses the model of Muneer and Kinghorn (1997), Kg = 136.6 - 74.541 Kt + 57.3421 Kt² in lm/W, where Kt is the clearness index: the global radiation over the radiation at the top of the atmosphere on a horizontal plane. The position of the sun at the sensor's coordinates, the date and the time, gives that ceiling, so the season and the hour are taken into account. There is no efficacy field to set. When the sun is lower than 5 degrees, or there are no coordinates, the middle of the range (113.7 lm/W) is used. A value stored by an older version is still honoured. Glass shifts the spectrum a little, which the model does not describe; the error stays within a few percent.

If you would rather not use this, a template sensor that converts your lux entity and is reported in W/m² reaches the same result through the radiation sensor source.

docs.title: Weather service history
docs.text: The weather service history, under Weather › Weather service, only shows values supplied by the weather service. A field whose source is a sensor appears as - there.

docs.title: Silent sensors
docs.text:
When a temperature, humidity, dew point, wind speed or pressure source of a sensor group stops reporting for more than 6 hours, Smart Irrigation says so instead of calculating on old data without a word. Every 15 minutes it looks at the groups that automatic zones use:

  • A notice appears in Settings › Repairs, one per sensor group, naming the silent sensors and since when. It disappears by itself when they report again.
  • The event smart_irrigation_weather_stale is fired once when a field goes silent, and smart_irrigation_weather_recovered once when it is back, so an automation can notify you. See the output contract.
  • A sensor counts as reporting when its entity state was updated. A field read from the weather service counts as reporting when the group last received data from it successfully.
  • Fields mapped to nothing or to a static value are not watched. After a restart of Home Assistant, a weather service is given the full 6 hours again before it can be called silent.

docs.title: Deleting a sensor group
docs.text: Use the button at the bottom of a group to delete it. Only a sensor group that no zone uses can be deleted.

docs.title: Setup assistant
docs.text:
The setup assistant exists because the other pages assume you already know what a sensor group is. It asks one question at a time, and only the questions your previous answers leave open, then creates the things a working zone needs.

It is not a tab: open it with Open the assistant, on its card under Settings › General, in the System section. Use it for a first zone, another one, or a fresh start.

You do not have to use it. Everything it does can be done by hand in the panel (zones under Zones, sensor groups under Weather › Sensor groups), and nothing it creates is locked afterwards.

docs.title: What it asks
docs.text:
What should Smart Irrigation do? Only for the first zone: Calculate and water (Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself, with a program) or Calculate only (your automation, Irrigation Unlimited or your controller opens them). See What Smart Irrigation does.

What are you watering? A name, the area, the flow, and the valve. The flow is the quantity of water this zone delivers per minute, and it is worth measuring rather than reading off a datasheet: every duration is computed from it, so an optimistic figure is the quietest way to water for twice as long as you think.

Where does it grow? Outdoors, or under glass or plastic. A greenhouse never receives rain, so saying so stops a rain forecast from holding back a watering the rain cannot reach, and hides the sources that would measure weather the plants never see.

Where should the evaporation figure come from? Four answers, in plain terms rather than by the name of the method behind them:

  • the weather service you configured, which needs nothing installed (offered once a weather service is on, and not under glass);
  • your own weather sensors;
  • a sensor that already reports evapotranspiration;
  • a fixed amount per day.

They map onto the three calculation modes, and the assistant picks the mode for you.

Which entities should it read? Only when your previous answer needs them, and only the sources the chosen mode actually reads. Choosing the weather service skips this step, except when the service is a weather entity of Home Assistant: it reports no rain that fell, so outdoors the assistant asks for a sensor that measures rain (the rate, or a gauge's total).

docs.title: What it creates
docs.text:
A calculation module, a sensor group and a zone, exactly as you would have created them by hand: modules, sensor groups and zones. The last step lists what is about to be created before anything is written.

Afterwards, the zone is an ordinary zone: change how it is calculated, point it at other sensors, add more zones to the same sensor group, or delete it.

docs.title: With Calculate and water
docs.text:
A zone is only watered once a program has it in a step, so the assistant puts a new zone with a valve in one:

  • with no program, it creates one, named Watering in your language, with that step and a schedule done by sunrise every day;
  • with one program, the zone becomes its last step;
  • with several, the last step of the assistant asks which one, or a new program.

The step takes the calculated duration. Change it, or move the zone to another program, under Watering › Programs.

docs.title: Weather configuration
docs.text:
The Weather tab gathers what Smart Irrigation reads the weather from, and everything that holds a run back. It has three pages:

  • Weather service: the weather service, then the location it is read for and how often it is read.
  • Sensor groups: which sensor or service provides each value the calculation reads, and above them, whether their sensors are recorded at every change (see sensor groups).
  • Skip watering: every check that can hold a run back, in one place: the rain forecast, the rain, frost and wind measured when a run starts, the days between irrigation, and a summary of what the zones set for themselves (soil moisture, days of their own).
Coming from an older version

The tab was called Data, and its pages keep their addresses. Before 2026.11.1 the Skip watering page was called Skip on weather, and the days between irrigation were under Settings › General.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
The weather is read for Home Assistant's location, unless you give other coordinates on the Location coordinates card: see manual coordinates.

Advanced mode

The card is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode once manual coordinates are on.

docs.title: Automatic weather data update
docs.text:
The weather is read every hour out of the box, which suits nearly every installation. The card has:

  • Automatically update weather data, on by default;
  • Read the weather every, in minutes, hours or days;
  • Delay before the first update, for sensors that do not have a value right after Home Assistant starts.

Advanced mode

The card is on the advanced panel. Once it is changed (switched off, another interval, or a delay), it shows in every mode, so a setting in use is never hidden.

A calculation works from the readings collected by these updates, so the weather must have been read at least once before the first calculation. With OpenWeatherMap or Pirate Weather, keep the interval at one hour or shorter: see sensor groups.

docs.title: Skipping a run
docs.text:
The checks below can hold a run back. They are all off by default.

When each check is judged.

  • What is measured is checked at each start, against what it reads then: the rain sensor, the frost, the wind, and your own postponement. A frost at 06:00 holds back the 06:00 run, not a program that starts at 18:00 on a mild evening.
  • What concerns the whole day is decided once, at the first start of the day, and kept for every later start that day: the rain forecast and the days between irrigation. A morning run resets the days since the last irrigation, and must not hold back the evening run for it.

A check that cannot be read, because its sensor is unavailable or the weather service does not answer, never stops a run: watering goes ahead as it would without it.

The Info page shows each check with its numbers: off, could not be checked, not blocking, or blocking. When a run is skipped, the smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped event fires with the reason. With Calculate and water, each schedule of a program can ignore the weather or apply only some of the checks.

Thresholds are entered in your unit system and a sensor is read in its own unit, so a sensor in °F works on a metric installation.

docs.title: Rain forecast
docs.text:
One switch, Take the forecast rain into account, and one threshold, Skip the run from. The threshold is 2 mm (about 0.08 inch) unless you set one. The rain counted is the rain you can expect, with each forecast weighted by its probability. Where the weather service has an hourly forecast, it is the rain of the 48 hours from the start of the run; otherwise it is the forecast for the day of the run and the next.

At or above the threshold the run is skipped, with two overrides so that a forecast that keeps missing does not dry a zone out: after 2 days in a row held back by the forecast, the run goes ahead; and when the rain expected is less than half (0.5) of the largest deficit among the zones that would water, it goes ahead too, because 3 mm of rain is no reason to hold back a zone 25 mm short. Zones in a greenhouse sensor group still water. Below the threshold, the run goes ahead and each zone is watered for less, as described next.

The panel keeps two settings behind the one switch (skip_irrigation_on_precipitation and forecast_rain_credit): the switch shows on when either is on, and turning it on or off sets both.

Below the threshold the duration is reduced in proportion. When a run starts, each zone is watered for the rain forecast to fall in the 24 hours after the start, less: the forecast hours are weighted by the probability the weather service gives, so 10 mm at 30% counts for 3 mm, and a forecast of 4 mm against a 10 mm deficit waters 6 mm. It works alongside the skip above, which stays all or nothing. A greenhouse zone is not reduced, and a forecast that cannot be read leaves the run as calculated.

Like the rain history below, it shortens the run and leaves the deficit in the water balance. The rain that really falls is measured and credited at the next calculation, so nothing is counted twice, and a forecast that does not come true is made up at the next run. The hours are counted from the moment the run starts, not from the calculation, which on a morning run is hours earlier. The forecast hours come from Open-Meteo, including for installations using another weather service.

docs.title: Rain sensor, freeze and wind
docs.text:
