The Skip on measured conditions card. Each check reads its sensor, or the weather service when you leave the sensor empty. Under the sensor of the freeze and wind checks, a line says what the check reads and whether a sensor group reads the same value for the evaporation; when a group reads it from another sensor, one tap makes the check read that sensor too.

  • Rain sensor. Skip while a binary sensor that is on in the rain says it is raining.
  • Freeze. Skip when the temperature is at or below the threshold, 2 °C (36 °F) unless you set one. It reads the sensor you choose, or the weather service's current temperature.
  • Wind. Skip when the wind is at or above the threshold, 20 km/h (12 mph) unless you set one: in strong wind a sprinkler waters the path, not the bed. It reads the sensor you choose, or the weather service's current wind. The weather service's wind is stored at 2 m for the evaporation, and taken back up to the 10 m that forecasts and wind limits are quoted at.

Shorten runs after recent rain. The rain sensor can do more than veto today: this reads its history over the last five days, weighted so that yesterday counts for more than four days ago, and shortens the run by the result. A day of reported rain today takes the whole run, four days ago takes a tenth of it, and a wet week takes everything.

Advanced mode

Shorten runs after recent rain is on the advanced panel, under the rain sensor.

It is for one case: a zone whose sensor group reports no rain in millimetres at all, neither a gauge's depth nor a service's rate. Where millimetres exist, the water balance already carries them and decides for itself how long rain keeps counting, and this stays out of the way.

It never touches the water balance, because it does not know how much fell. The deficit stays where it was and is watered once the weather turns, which is the safe direction: a run shortened too much is made up tomorrow, while water that was never owed cannot be taken back out of the ground. It needs a sensor that stays on while it rains; one that pulses briefly per bucket tip spends almost no time on and will barely register.

The idea of weighting rain over a few rolling days comes from kloggy's HA-Irrigation-Version2 package, which does it with history_stats over five 24-hour windows.

docs.title: Soil moisture
docs.text:
Soil moisture is set on each zone rather than here, since each zone has its own sensor. The page lists the zones that have one, with their threshold, each a link to its zone.

Give a zone a soil moisture sensor and a threshold in %, 50 unless you set one, and while the reading is at or above it that zone sits the run out and the others water. Its duration for that run goes to 0 and its water balance is kept, so the deficit rolls over to the next run.

Every calculation applies the same rule: a zone whose soil reads at or above its threshold has its water balance set to field capacity, so the deficit shown never contradicts the sensor between two starts.

It works in that direction only. A dry reading says nothing about how many millimetres are missing without a calibration of the sensor to the soil, and a deficit invented from one would water a zone for good on the strength of a badly placed probe.

docs.title: Days between irrigation
docs.text:
The Days between irrigation card, with Minimum days between irrigation: the fewest calendar days between two waterings. 0, the default, is no limit: watering can happen every day it is needed. Set to N, watering happens at most every N days (up to 365). It is useful for:

  • water conservation: time enough between waterings;
  • plant health: the soil dries a little between waterings;
  • local restrictions: a watering schedule you have to keep.

For example, 1 allows watering every day, 3 every third day, and 7 once a week.

The days since the last watering are counted once per calendar day, at midnight, whether or not watering happened that day. A start that comes too early is skipped and the count goes on; the first start once enough days have passed waters, and the count starts again from 0. The rain forecast and this check both have to allow a run for it to happen.

Different days for one zone. A zone can have its own number, in the Days between irrigation field of its settings. The card lists the zones that have days of their own, each a link to its zone.

  • That number replaces this setting for that zone alone, so a lawn can wait three days while the flower beds are watered every day. Leave the zone's field empty to follow this setting.
  • The general count only restarts when a zone that follows it is watered, so a zone with days of its own, watered every day, does not keep the others from ever being due.
  • The day is only skipped as a whole when every zone is still within its days. Otherwise the run goes ahead for the zones that are due, and the others sit it out.

Advanced mode

The zone's field is on the advanced panel, and shows in every mode once it is set.

docs.title: Zone configuration
docs.text:
A zone is one part of the garden watered by one valve (or several opened together). Create as many as you have, each with its own area and flow. The duration of each zone is calculated from its water balance, its module and its sensor group.

A zone is in one of three states:

  • Automatic: Smart Irrigation calculates the duration from the water balance and waters at the start. It needs a sensor group.
  • Manual: you set the duration yourself, in minutes. Every start waters the zone for that duration, whatever its water balance. No sensor group is needed.
  • Disabled: never watered, and its water balance is not followed. Its duration is 0.

Units

Take note of the unit shown beside each field, so you enter values in the right one. Metric and imperial follow the unit system of Home Assistant.

docs.title: Adding a zone
docs.text:
Under Zones, the Add zone card asks for:

  • Name: the name of the zone, for example "Lawn";
  • Size: the area it waters, in m² or sq ft;
  • Throughput: its flow, in litres or gallons per minute.

Add zone creates it, and Set it up with the assistant opens the setup assistant instead. Each zone becomes a set of entities in Home Assistant. Then configure the rest of the zone, below.

docs.title: Actions on all zones
docs.text:
The Actions on all zones card acts on every automatic zone:

  • Update all zones: read the weather for the sensor groups of the automatic zones.
  • Calculate all zones: calculate the duration of every automatic zone. The weather data used is deleted afterwards.
  • Reset all water balances: set every automatic zone's water balance to 0.
  • Clear all weather data: delete the weather data collected for the sensor groups of the automatic zones.

The last two discard data of every zone, and each asks first.

docs.title: Configuring a zone
docs.text:
To configure a zone, you need its flow (throughput) and the area it waters (size). If you do not know them, enter its precipitation rate (in mm/h or in/h) instead. To measure it, place a straight-sided container in the zone, water for exactly one hour, and measure the depth of water collected: that depth is the precipitation rate.

Every field of a zone has a short hint under it in the panel. For a manual zone, the line under the zone name shows its duration and litres; an automatic zone does not show it. The status band of an automatic zone reads the live estimate: "Short by X mm: about N min (V L) at the next calculation" when the estimate gives a duration, "Will water ... at the next start" when a stored duration exists, "Nothing to water" with the deficit under the zone's threshold, or "has what it needs".

You can change the following settings on a zone:

  • Name: the name of the zone.
  • Input method: how the water delivered is known:
    • Throughput & area (default): the rate is calculated from Size and Throughput.
    • Precipitation rate: you enter the rate directly.
  • Size and Throughput: used with Throughput & area.
  • Precipitation rate: used with Precipitation rate.
  • Drainage rate: how fast a saturated root zone drains, in mm/h, which is the soil's saturated hydraulic conductivity. It only applies when bucket > 0, meaning the soil is above field capacity. It is the full rate at saturation, when the water balance reaches the maximum water balance; below that it falls steeply with how much surplus is left, following Brooks and Corey, Eq. 4-6. The drainage over a calculation is worked out from that rate law exactly, so a surplus drains quickly at first and more and more slowly as it empties. Indicative values, from the texture-class averages in Rawls, Brakensiek and Saxton (1982): about 210 mm/h for sand, 60 for loamy sand, 26 for sandy loam, 13 for loam, 7 for silt loam, 2 for clay loam and under 1 mm/h for clay. A new zone starts at 8 mm/h, loam in the panel's soil list. Zones made earlier started at 50.8 mm/h, which is fast for most garden soils, and keep it. Either starting value reads as "Not chosen yet", with the number, until a soil is picked or a rate typed. The field appears right under Soil only when the soil is "I set the drainage myself", in both modes: a soil chosen by name stands for its rate. A drainage rate of 0 means a surplus never drains: rain above field capacity then stays in the water balance until evaporation removes it, and the next irrigation is delayed by however many days that takes.
  • State: Automatic, Manual or Disabled, described at the top of this page.

  • Evapotranspiration: how this zone's water need is worked out, in three answers:

    • Calculated by Smart Irrigation, from your measurements (temperature, humidity, wind, sun), with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith;
    • Provided by a sensor or a service, when you already have an evapotranspiration in millimetres, taken as it is;
    • A fixed amount, so many mm a day whatever the weather.

    The module behind your answer is created and reused for you, one per zone: there is nothing to create by hand and no module to choose. On the advanced panel, the module's own settings appear with it: Look ahead, the number of days to come averaged into today's need (0 by default), and Coastal site, for a zone calculated by Smart Irrigation; Evaporation per day, a positive number of mm, for a zone that uses a fixed amount. Each zone has its own, so changing them here changes nothing anywhere else. - Sensor group: Choose the sensor group that provides the weather data for this zone. - Water balance: calculated, or set by hand. Negative, the zone is short of water; zero or above, it has what it needs. A deficit only leads to watering once it reaches the zone's Irrigation threshold (below). See how it works. - Maximum water balance: how much water the root zone can hold above field capacity before it is saturated, so it only applies when bucket > 0. Anything beyond it runs off, and it is the saturation reference the drainage curve is scaled by. It is not the total water your soil holds for the plant, and it never changes when a zone starts watering.

    Physically it is (saturation - field capacity) x root depth: the soil's drainable porosity over the depth the roots use. The same averages give about 0.35 for sand, 0.19 for loam and 0.08 for clay, so for a 20 cm root zone roughly 70 mm for sand, 40 mm for loam and 15 mm for clay. Take them as a starting point: they move with how field capacity is defined, and a real soil is not a class average.

    Sand gets the larger value, not the smaller. Its big pores hold a lot of water for the short while it takes to drain and little once it has; clay is the reverse. Earlier versions of this page gave 30 mm for clay and 12 mm for sand. Those are closer to the available water capacity, which belongs to the other way of counting soil water, and they are inverted for this one. See discussion #783 for how this was worked out.

  • Lead time: the time your system needs before water arrives, in seconds: to connect, start a pump, build pressure. It is added to a calculated duration above 0.
  • Maximum duration: the longest run of the zone, to avoid flooding or waste. When one run at this duration cannot make up what the zone loses between two waterings (a drip line capped at ten minutes with three days between waterings, say), Smart Irrigation raises a repair issue naming the zone: its deficit would otherwise grow for good. It is advice, and clears itself once the zone can keep up.

  • Crop factor (Kc): the factor between the reference evapotranspiration and what the planting uses. The field appears right under What grows here only when that choice is "I set the crop factor myself". It scales the evapotranspiration to the water your crop actually uses, ETc = ET0 * Kc, so the water balance is depleted at the crop's rate rather than the reference one. It is applied to the evapotranspiration and not to the rain that fell on it, nor to the resulting duration. For lawns, it is recommended to set the crop factor depending on your grass type (See this discussion for more details):

    • cool-season grasses (such as fescue, bluegrass): 0.8;
    • warm-season grasses (such as bermuda, zoysia): 0.7.

    It carries plant density too, not just species. The reference the calculation starts from is a continuous grass surface, so the figure quoted for a species assumes it covers the ground. A zone that does not is using less water per square metre than that figure says, because there is less leaf there to lose it. A hedge on a drip line, measured over the strip its emitters wet, is close to full cover once it has grown together and the species figure is about right. A young or widely spaced planting is not, and its factor should come down roughly in proportion to how much of the zone the canopy actually shades. The landscape literature writes this as the species factor multiplied by a density factor, which is the same idea.

    This is why the area you enter and the crop factor have to describe the same patch of ground. If you take the whole bed as the area for a drip line, you are claiming a canopy over all of it; if you take the wetted strip, you are claiming one over the strip, which for an established hedge is true. Either can be made correct, but not by mixing one area with the other's factor.

    A dry spell waters the same as it always did: the crop factor ends up multiplying the same total either way. What changes is a period with rain, where a factor below 1 used to credit only that fraction of the millimetres that fell and therefore over-watered, and the moment irrigation becomes necessary, which now arrives at the crop's rate of depletion rather than about 1/Kc times too early. - Soil: the soil of the zone by name (sandy, sandy loam, loam, clay loam, clay), which stands for its drainage rate (see Drainage rate above). Choose "I set the drainage rate myself" to type the rate. A zone nobody chose a soil for reads "Not chosen yet:" and its starting rate; choosing that again puts the zone back on 8 mm/h. - What grows here: the planting by name (lawn, vegetables, flowers, shrubs, hedge, fruit trees, vines, ground cover), which stands for its crop factor. Choose "I set the crop factor myself" to type the Crop factor (Kc) above. A zone nobody chose a planting for reads "Not chosen yet: factor 1.0". - Soil moisture sensor and Skip at or above (advanced mode; once a sensor is set, they show in every mode): a sensor of the soil of this zone and the % from which the zone sits out a run. See Skipping a run. - Linked valve/switch: the valve or switch that waters this zone. It is what observed watering watches, and what Smart Irrigation opens with Calculate and water. It can be linked once Calculate and water or observed watering is on. - Other valves of the zone, Pump or main valve: valves opened and closed together with the linked one, and the supply that feeds the zone (Calculate and water). - Wait for the valve to confirm, the safety off fields, Valve's own duration and If the valve's own timer can't be set (advanced mode, with Calculate and water and a linked valve): see when Smart Irrigation runs the valves and hardware auto-off. - Ignore runs up to (advanced mode): see leave short runs out. - Cumulative volume meter: a water-meter total for the zone, for exact crediting instead of throughput x time. See the volume meter. - Days between irrigation (advanced mode; once set, it shows in every mode): the minimum number of calendar days between two waterings of this zone alone. Empty, the default, follows the general days between irrigation setting, which is what every installation did before this field existed. A number replaces the general setting for this zone: 1 waters it every day it needs water, 3 at most every third day, 0 removes the restriction for it. The days are counted from the last time this zone was watered, and the zone's deficit keeps building while it waits, so it is made up at the next run. Useful when one garden holds a lawn that wants infrequent deep watering and flower beds that want water daily. - Crop factor by month (advanced mode): for a crop whose water use follows its growth, the crop factor (Kc) of each month, January first. A month left empty uses the crop factor of the zone, and twelve empty months are that crop factor all year, as before. A lawn can read 0.6 in March, 0.9 in June and 0.5 in November without a single adjustment to create. Seasonal adjustments still apply on top, as a multiplier of the factor of the month. - Available water and allowed depletion (advanced mode): what the soil of the zone holds for the plants, in mm, and the share of it the plants may use up before they suffer. Empty, the default, leaves the water balance exactly as it was: the deficit grows for as long as it does not rain. Set the available water (the root depth in metres times what the soil holds per metre of depth, about 50 to 110 mm for sand, 130 to 180 mm for loam and 120 to 200 mm for clay according to FAO-56, Table 19, so a lawn rooted at 0.15 m on loam holds about 20 to 27 mm) and two things change. The deficit cannot go below it, because a soil cannot be drier than that, and once the deficit passes the allowed share of it (50% unless you change it) the plants draw less water, falling to nothing as the soil empties (the FAO-56 stress coefficient). A zone watered in time never reaches that point, so the figure matters most after a long dry spell or a missed run, where it stops the water balance from showing a deficit no plant could have used. The threshold below stays in mm and is not tied to it. - Distribution efficiency (advanced mode): the share of the water leaving the emitters that reaches the plants, in %. Empty is 100%: the throughput is taken at its word, as before. A zone at 80% waters 25% longer for the same depth, and credits the water balance with only 80% of what it delivers, whether it is timed, observed or metered. Sprinklers in wind or on a slope lose some; drip loses almost none. - Irrigation threshold: how much of a soil moisture deficit to let build up before watering at all, in mm or inch. 0, the default, waters as soon as anything is missing, which is what every installation did before this setting existed; it is not what agronomy recommends for anything, a lawn included. Set a threshold and the zone stays dry until that much water is owed, then delivers all of it in one deep run: a lawn wants a small one because its roots are shallow, a tree or a hedge a large one. It changes when a zone waters, not how much: once the threshold is reached the run still covers the whole deficit. It follows that a zone never waters less than its threshold, so it also rules out very short runs. In soil terms this is the management allowed depletion (MAD).

To pick a value, work from the water your soil actually holds for the plant, the total available water: TAW = available water capacity of the soil x root depth. As a rough guide the available water capacity runs about 50 to 110 mm per metre in sand, 130 to 180 in loam and 120 to 200 in clay (FAO-56, Table 19), and the root depth is what matters for that planting, perhaps 0.15 to 0.3 m for turf and a metre or more for an established tree. The threshold is then a fraction of that, p x TAW, with p around 0.5 as a starting point (FAO-56 gives per-crop values, mostly between 0.4 and 0.6). A lawn on loam at 0.2 m therefore lands somewhere near 15 mm.

Do not derive it from the Maximum water balance: that setting caps the surplus above field capacity, which is the other side of zero and a different quantity entirely.

The default of 0 is there to keep existing installs behaving exactly as before, not because watering the instant anything is missing is good practice. Deep and infrequent watering suits a lawn too; it simply wants a smaller threshold than a tree because its roots are shallower.

docs.title: Zone actions
docs.text:
Each zone's card also has:

  • Calculate, Update (read its weather) and Reset water balance;
  • Water, with Calculate and water and a linked valve: waters the zone now (see watering one zone by hand);
  • View weather data: the last 10 records of its sensor group;
  • View watering calendar: a 12-month watering estimate from the location and typical weather;
  • Delete.

docs.title: A zone in YAML
docs.text:
The Edit in YAML icon in a zone's header row shows its settings as text, in place of the form, and back, as for a program. The numbers are in the units the panel shows. Only settings are written: what the calculation and the runs write (water balance, duration, explanation, last calculation, measured throughput...) is not, and cannot be set there. An optional setting you remove is cleared; a required one (name, size, state...) is kept. Nothing is saved until Apply, which saves only what changed, the same way the form does; a key that is not a zone setting, or a value the zone refuses, is named under the editor.

name: Front lawn
state: automatic
size: 50
throughput: 12
linked_entity: valve.front_lawn
safety_off_topic: zigbee2mqtt/front_lawn_valve/set
safety_off_state_key: state_l1
open_resends: 0

YAML only: two zone options

These have no field in the form, even when they are set. Editing the zone in the form keeps them, and a zone that uses one says so in a Set in YAML (not editable here) box, with Edit in YAML at hand:

  • safety_off_state_key: state_l1, the safety off state key (empty is state);
  • open_resends: 0, how often the open is sent again while the valve has not confirmed (0 to 10; empty is the default).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Smart Irrigation is configured in its own panel, Smart Irrigation in the Home Assistant sidebar. Install it first.

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text:
The panel has four tabs, five with Calculate and water. Each is a group of pages: a tab opens its first page and shows the others on a second row.

  1. Home: what is happening. Info says what will happen at the next start and why, whether it would be held back, where each zone stands right now, and the days ahead. History says what actually ran, by day, with durations and volumes.
  2. Zones: the zones of your irrigation system: what each waters, how it is calculated, and what it is short of.
  3. Watering, with Calculate and water only: Planning, Programs, and Pumps and valves. See Watering with programs.
  4. Weather: where the numbers come from, and what holds a run back. See Weather configuration:
    • Weather service: the weather service, the location it is read for and how often it is read;
    • Sensor groups: which sensor or service provides each value the calculation reads (sensor groups);
    • Skip watering: every check that can hold a run back, the days between irrigation included.
  5. Settings: what you set once. General: what Smart Irrigation does (Calculate and water, Calculate only, or Stop everything), then the calculation, the control and the system. Then Backup / restore, and Help.

Two pages are in no tab, and open from a card of Settings › General:

  • the setup assistant, for a first zone, another one, or a fresh start;
  • the import from Irrigation Unlimited.

There is no modules page any more: a zone says how it is calculated, and the module behind that answer is created and reused for you.

Coming from an older version

The panel used to have ten tabs. The Weather tab was called Data, and the Skip watering page was called Skip on weather until 2026.11.1. The pages kept their addresses.

docs.title: Standard and advanced
docs.text:
The panel comes in two depths, switched by Advanced settings under Settings › General, in the System section.

The standard panel keeps what a zone is: its name, what it waters with, where its weather comes from, what it is short of. The advanced panel adds the settings that tune the model (the drainage rate, the thresholds, the crop factor, how far ahead a zone looks...). They have sound defaults and are not improved by being met by accident. These pages mark them like this:

Advanced mode

A setting shown only on the advanced panel. Once it is changed from its default, most of them show in every mode, so a setting in use is never hidden.

An installation that already had zones when the two depths arrived is on the advanced panel, because those settings were chosen on purpose. A fresh installation starts on the standard one. Either way the choice is yours, and nothing is lost in either direction: the settings keep their values.

docs.title: Set in YAML
docs.text:
A few options for power users have no field in the panel at all. Programs and zones have Edit in YAML, which shows them as text, and these options are written there. These pages mark them like this:

YAML only

An option with no field in the form. Editing in the form keeps it, and a program or a zone that uses one lists it in a Set in YAML (not editable here) box, with Edit in YAML at hand.

The list is under YAML-only options, and every key of a program is in its reference.

See also: Closed-loop watering, which credits the water balance from real watering and covers what happens at the valve.

docs.title: From nothing to a watered garden
docs.text:
This is the whole path, for somebody who has none of it yet: a machine, a valve, Home Assistant, Smart Irrigation, and a zone that waters itself on what the weather took out of the soil. Half an hour of work, most of it waiting for downloads.

It is deliberately the shortest path that is still correct. Every step links to the page that goes deeper, and nothing here has to be undone later.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Something to run Home Assistant on. A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 is the usual answer, with a decent SD card or, better, an SSD. Any machine on Home Assistant's installation page works, including an old laptop or a virtual machine.

A way to open and close the water. Two routes, and the choice matters more than anything else on this page:

How it works Watch out for A wireless valve (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) Battery or mains valve that screws onto a tap and appears in Home Assistant as a valve or switch. Zigbee and Z-Wave need a coordinator stick. Battery life over a season, and range from the house to the garden. A relay board driving solenoid valves Irrigation solenoids (commonly 24 V AC) wired to a relay board, which Home Assistant switches. This is what a multi-zone garden ends up with. Mains and water in the same box: use a proper enclosure and a transformer rated for your valves, and have an electrician do it if you are not sure.

We do not sell or endorse hardware, and this page names no models on purpose: what matters is that the valve appears in Home Assistant as something you can turn on and off.

Weather data. No hardware needed: Open-Meteo is free and needs no account. Your own sensors are better if you have them, and you can add them later without starting over.

Numbers about your garden. Two, per zone, and you can measure them in ten minutes:

  • the area it waters, in m² or sq ft;
  • the flow, in litres or gallons per minute. Time how long your sprinkler takes to fill a bucket of known volume: a 10 litre bucket in 40 seconds is 15 L/min.

If you would rather not, the panel also takes a precipitation rate in mm/h directly, which is what a sprinkler manufacturer's data sheet gives.

docs.title: 1. Home Assistant (15 minutes, mostly unattended)
docs.text:
Follow Home Assistant's own installation guide for your machine and pick Home Assistant OS if you have the choice: it is the version that supports add-ons and updates itself, and it is the one every instruction you will read assumes.

On a Raspberry Pi, the steps are these. Home Assistant's own guide has the details and is the reference if anything differs.

  1. On another computer, install the Raspberry Pi Imager.
  2. In the Imager, choose your Pi model, then the operating system under Other specific-purpose OS, Home assistants and home automation, Home Assistant, and the version for your model. Choose the SD card or SSD, and write it. If you use an SSD, your Pi needs to be set up to boot from USB; the Imager and the Raspberry Pi documentation say how.
  3. Put the card or drive in the Pi, plug in the network cable (a cable is easier than Wi-Fi the first time) and the power. The first start downloads and prepares Home Assistant and takes a while, often twenty minutes. Nothing is wrong if the page is not there yet.
  4. From a computer on the same network, open http://homeassistant.local:8123 (or the Pi's address from your router) and follow the on-screen setup.

When it is up, create your account, set your location, time zone and elevation properly. Smart Irrigation needs them: the sun's position at your latitude is half of the evapotranspiration equation.

docs.title: 2. Your valve, in Home Assistant (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Add the valve the way its own integration asks (a Zigbee stick and ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT for a Zigbee valve, the brand's integration for a Wi-Fi one, a GPIO or Modbus integration for a relay board).

Then prove it works, before Smart Irrigation is anywhere near it: in Developer tools › Actions, call switch.turn_on (or valve.open_valve) on that entity and watch the water. Turn it off again. If that does not work, nothing later will, and it will look like our fault.

Write the entity id down, switch.garden_tap or whatever it is.

docs.title: 3. Smart Irrigation (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Install HACS if you do not have it, then:

  1. In HACS, search for Smart Irrigation, download it.
  2. Restart Home Assistant.
  3. Settings › Devices & services › Add integration, search for Smart Irrigation.
  4. Confirm: setup asks nothing. The weather service is chosen later, in the panel: Open-Meteo needs nothing; OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather ask for a free API key.

The full version of this step, including the manual install and what to do when HACS does not find it, is on the installation page.

docs.title: 4. The first zone (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Open Smart Irrigation in the sidebar. To use a weather service, turn it on first: on Weather › Weather service, switch on Use a weather service, keep Open-Meteo and save. Then open the setup assistant (Settings › General, Open the assistant). It asks a few questions, one at a time:

  1. What should Smart Irrigation do? Calculate and water if Smart Irrigation should open the valve itself, Calculate only if your own automation or controller will (step 5 explains both).
  2. What are you watering? A name, the area and the flow you measured, and the valve: the entity from step 2.
  3. Where does it grow? Outdoors, or under glass or plastic.
  4. Where should the evaporation figure come from? The weather service is the simplest answer. It is only offered once a weather service is on.
  5. Which entities should it read?, only when your answers need sensors.

It creates the sensor group and the first zone for you. Then, on the zone's card under Zones, say what the soil is and what grows there, in words. Those two set the drainage rate and the crop factor behind them (FAO-56 values), which nobody can answer in millimetres an hour.

You now have a zone that computes a duration every night at 23:00.

docs.title: 5. Make the water actually flow (2 minutes)
docs.text:
This is the step people skip, and then nothing waters: Smart Irrigation decides how long, and something has to do it. Two ways.

Let Smart Irrigation do it: Calculate and water. If you chose it in the assistant and gave the zone its valve, it is done: the zone is a step of a program called Watering, which waters it every day, done by sunrise. The program opens the valve, waits the calculated duration, closes it, and credits the zone itself. Nothing else to write. You find it under Watering › Programs. If you chose Calculate only first, set the zone's Linked valve/switch under Zones, then choose Calculate and water in Settings › General: with no program yet, it creates one with every zone that has a valve.

Give your valve a hardware failsafe

If Home Assistant goes down in the middle of a run, nothing here can close the valve. Give it a maximum run time on the device itself if it has one: see hardware auto-off.

Or keep your own automation: Calculate only. An import-ready blueprint does it for a plain switch, for Irrigation Unlimited, or for a Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler or B-hyve controller. Turn the controller's own schedule off if it has one, or it will water twice.

Either way, the Home page tells you whether an installation would ever water, and names the reason when it would not.

docs.title: 6. Check it, tonight and tomorrow
docs.text:
• Home page: what happens next, and what would hold it back. It answers in one sentence.
  • With Calculate and water, press Water on the zone's card under Zones, or add the dashboard card and press its drop: two taps, and you should hear water.
  • Tomorrow morning, the zone's calculation explanation shows the night's numbers: what was read, what evaporated, what rain was credited, and the duration it produced.

docs.title: After a week
docs.text:
Change one thing at a time, and let a few days pass before judging it.

  • It waters too often, in short runs. Raise the zone's irrigation threshold: the deficit it lets build up before watering at all. Deep and infrequent is better for almost everything, a lawn included; the zones page has the arithmetic for picking a number from your soil and root depth.
  • It waters too much or too little overall. The crop factor is the honest knob (the what grows here choice sets it), not the duration. Check the flow you measured first.
  • The ground stays soaked. Your soil cannot take it that fast: water in several passes with a soak between them. With Calculate and water, that is Water in several passes on the zone's step, under Watering › Programs. With Calculate only, your own automation or controller does it.
  • Nothing happens at all. Troubleshooting, then an issue with a diagnostics file, which is the fastest way to a real answer.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• How it works: the water balance, in plain terms.
  • Which weather service, and what each one gives you.
  • Zone configuration: every setting on a zone and what it does.
  • Watering with programs: programs, schedules, pumps and main valves, with Calculate and water.
  • Closed-loop watering: crediting from real runs, and what happens at the valve.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
One word for each thing in the panel, and these pages use the same words. The code, the services, the entity ids and the attributes keep their own names, so automations that use them do not change. The column "In code" gives that name.

When you translate the panel, use the word in the second or third column for the thing in the first; a language without a column yet is free to pick its word, as long as it keeps to one.

What it is Panel (English) Panel (German) In code The water a zone's root zone has, counted from field capacity, in mm (or inches). Zero means it holds what it can; below zero it is short, above zero there is a surplus that drains away. Water balance Wasserbilanz bucket What a zone is short of, the water balance below zero, as a positive amount. Deficit Defizit (negative bucket) The largest surplus a zone keeps above field capacity. Maximum water balance Maximale Wasserbilanz maximum_bucket How fast a saturated root zone drains, in mm/h. Drainage rate Entwässerungsrate drainage_rate The water lost to evaporation and plants. ET0 is the reference value from the weather, ETc that value times the crop factor. Evapotranspiration (ET0, ETc) Evapotranspiration (ET0, ETc) (none) The factor between ET0 and what the planting uses. Crop factor (Kc) Pflanzenfaktor (Kc) multiplier The way a zone's water loss is calculated: from the weather (PyETO), a fixed amount (Static), or a value another sensor provides (Passthrough). Module Modul module The sources a zone reads its weather from: a weather service, your own sensors, or both. Sensor group Sensorgruppe mapping An online service that provides weather data and forecasts. Weather service Wetterdienst weather_service How long a zone is watered at the next start, worked out from its water balance and its flow. Duration Dauer duration With Calculate only, when the start event fires: a time, sunrise or sunset, or the sun's position. Start trigger Startauslöser irrigation_start_triggers What Smart Irrigation does: open the valves itself with its programs, only calculate, or nothing. Calculate and water, Calculate only, Stop everything Berechnen und bewässern, Nur berechnen, Alles anhalten mode: water, calculate, off An ordered list of steps that waters zones, started by its schedules (with Calculate and water). Program Programm programs One zone, or several watered together, in a program. Step Schritt steps When a program starts: a moment and the days it applies to. Schedule Zeitplan schedules A pump or a main valve that runs while a zone it feeds is watered. Pump or main valve Pumpe oder Hauptventil supplies A soil or planting nobody picked: the zone is calculated with the value it started with. Not chosen yet Noch nicht gewählt soil_type / plant_type empty

docs.title: Words that are not used
docs.text:
Instead of Say bucket (in a text), Vorrat, Eimer water balance, Wasserbilanz full controller, master switch Calculate and water, What Smart Irrigation does engine, calculation engine, Berechnungs-Engine module, Modul mapping (in a text) sensor group, Sensorgruppe crop coefficient, multiplier, Pflanzenkoeffizient, Multiplikator crop factor, Pflanzenfaktor

"bucket" stays where it is code: the attribute bucket, the action set_bucket (and, until they go in 2027.11, set_all_buckets, reset_bucket and reset_all_buckets), and the entity ids ending in _bucket.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Start with the documentation: installation, configuration (zones, sensor groups, weather), watering with programs, entities, events, services and troubleshooting.

Prefer video? Watch the tutorial playlist on YouTube (English) or this community tutorial in German.

Still stuck? Browse the Discussions and the Home Assistant community thread.

If that does not help, open an issue, with a diagnostics file (see troubleshooting).

docs.title: Help translate
docs.text:
The panel and the names Home Assistant shows for the integration (entities, buttons, services, the setup dialog) come in 20 languages. Apart from English and French, those translations were machine-made and nobody who speaks the language has read them yet, so some will read oddly.

If yours does, you can fix it on Hosted Weblate, in the browser: pick the language, correct the string, save. No Git, no build tools. The corrections reach the repository as a pull request and ship with the next release. One word in one string is a welcome contribution.

A few rules keep a translation working, and Weblate checks most of them for you:

  • Keep every placeholder as it is, such as {count} or {duration}: the integration fills them in.
  • Reuse the words the panel already uses for the same idea, so a user reads one word on every screen.
  • Leave a string untranslated rather than guess. An untranslated string shows in English, an empty one shows nothing.

Your language is not in the list? Ask on Weblate or open an issue: a new language needs a small change in the panel as well as its translation. Prefer editing the files directly? The contribution guide explains how.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The picture below shows what Smart Irrigation does. The words for each part, as the panel uses them, are in the glossary.

  1. Rain and snow add water to the ground: the precipitation.
  2. Sun, temperature, humidity, wind and the place on earth decide how much water leaves the ground and the leaves: the evapotranspiration.
  3. The difference between the two is the net precipitation (the delta). Negative, more water was lost than the rain brought; positive, the rain brought more than was lost.
  4. At each calculation, the net precipitation is added to the zone's water balance (the bucket attribute), which starts at zero: new water balance = old water balance + net precipitation.

  5. Above zero, the soil holds more than it can keep, and the surplus drains. The drainage rate falls as the surplus empties, following the hydraulic conductivity of Brooks and Corey, Eq. 4-6, scaled by the maximum water balance.

    When it rained during the period, the period is replayed hour by hour: each hour gets its evapotranspiration, the rain that fell in it, then that hour's drainage. The evapotranspiration of each hour is the hourly equation's own figure when the hourly calculation is on, and otherwise follows the sun (in proportion to how high it stands, nothing at night). A rain that just fell only drains from the hour it fell, not as if it had been in the soil since the previous calculation. When the rain fell is taken from the readings of the rain sensor (a rain gauge's total, or a rain rate); when nothing says it, the rain is spread evenly over the period.

  6. Below zero, the zone is short of water: watering is needed.

  7. The zone waters for sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] seconds. That is 0 when the water balance is zero or above, or when the deficit is below the zone's irrigation threshold: deep and infrequent beats a daily trickle.

  8. Afterwards, the water balance is credited with the water that went in. Three ways, and you pick one:

    • let Smart Irrigation open the valve itself (Calculate and water), which credits the runs it makes;
    • let it watch the valve (observed watering) and credit any run of it;
    • call credit_watering from your own automation with how long the zone ran. A blueprint does it for you, per brand of controller.

    Never two of them, or the water is counted twice.

The whole of what is published and when it changes is on one page: the output contract.

docs.title: What the crop needs, not what a lawn of grass would
docs.text:
The evapotranspiration the equation computes is a reference: what a short, well-watered grass surface would lose. A hedge, a vegetable bed and a lawn do not lose the same, and the difference is the crop factor Kc, which is the zone's crop factor setting:

ETc = ET0 x Kc

It is applied to the evapotranspiration, before the water balance. That order matters, and it is worth saying why, because it used to be the other way round: the factor was applied at the very end, to the duration. That scaled the whole balance rather than the crop's water use, so a factor below 1 credited only that fraction of the rain that fell, and the water balance kept draining at the full reference rate, reaching any threshold about 1/Kc times too fast. No factor applied at the end can undo a decision about when to water.

The panel asks what grows in the zone, in words, and writes the FAO-56 factor for the answer. Your own number wins if you set one.

docs.title: Hour by hour, or once a day
docs.text:
The equation exists in two forms, and both are FAO-56.

The daily form runs once over the whole window, on its averages. The hourly form prices each hour of the window and adds them up. They are not the same number, because evapotranspiration is not linear in its terms: a cool humid night and a hot dry afternoon priced separately do not give what their averages give, and the separate answer is the right one. The daily equation is an average of a curve.

A new installation starts on the hourly form. One that existed before it arrived keeps the daily one until its owner switches, because the two give different numbers and nobody's watering should change on an update. The switch is under Settings › General, and what each form needs is documented there.

Either way the sun is the term the result is most sensitive to. A radiation sensor is best, a weather service that publishes radiation is next, and the day's temperature range is the last resort: the estimate FAO-56 gives for exactly that case.

docs.title: A week, as an example
docs.text:
To see how the precipitation, the net precipitation, the water balance and the watering work together, here is one zone over a week. Use it to check your own configuration. The values are made up and only show the mechanism.

At the start, the water balance is 0, so the duration is 0 seconds.

docs.title: Variables used
docs.text:
• P: precipitation
  • Et: evapotranspiration
  • D: net precipitation, or delta (P - Et)
  • B: water balance
  • Bu: water balance after the calculation (B + D)
  • Du: watering duration, in seconds

docs.title: When to water
docs.text:
For most plants, a lawn included, deep and infrequent watering is better than a little every day: it encourages deep roots. Smart Irrigation does that with two settings rather than an automation of your own:

  • the zone's irrigation threshold, the deficit it lets build up before watering at all (see zones, which explains how to pick a number from your soil and root depth);
  • the days between irrigation, the fewest days between two waterings (see Skip watering).

docs.title: With HACS (recommended)
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation is in the HACS default store, and HACS handles the updates. Open it in HACS in one click:

or search for Smart Irrigation in the HACS panel. Then click Download.

If you added this repository as a custom repository in the past, that entry is no longer needed.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text: Download the latest release as a zip file and extract it into the custom_components folder of your Home Assistant configuration. You should end up with custom_components/smart_irrigation/.

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. Restart Home Assistant to load the integration.
  2. Go to Settings › Devices & services › Add integration, search for Smart Irrigation and add it.
  3. Confirm with OK: setup asks nothing. Open the Smart Irrigation panel in the sidebar, turn on the weather service if you want one, and let the setup assistant create your first zone (see Installation).

docs.title: Migrating from V1 (0.0.X) to V2
docs.text:
Only for very old installations

This page is for an installation still on version 0.0.X. Any later version updates normally: see Updating.

Version 2 is a complete rewrite of the integration. It fixes many bugs of V1, supports several zones in one installation, and is more accurate and more flexible. In V1, each zone needed its own instance of Smart Irrigation; V2 allows only one instance, with as many zones as you need.

There is no automatic upgrade path from V1 to V2. Follow these steps for each V1 instance before you upgrade:

  1. Make sure you are on V0.0.82 or later.
  2. In Home Assistant, go to Settings › Devices & services › Smart Irrigation, or use this link.

  3. For each instance of Smart Irrigation, choose Download diagnostics in the three-dot menu.

      "source": "user",
      "unique_id": "Smart Irrigation",
      "disabled_by": null
    }
  }
}

  6. Once you have downloaded and checked a diagnostics file for each instance, remove all instances of Smart Irrigation.

  7. Restart Home Assistant.
  8. Install the current Smart Irrigation with HACS (see Installation). To keep using OpenWeatherMap, use your API key; your diagnostics file also reminds you which sensors supplied part of the weather data.
  9. Set up your zones in the Smart Irrigation panel, using the diagnostics file. A few things have changed:
    • Reference ET values are no longer needed.
    • Each zone has a Throughput: number_of_sprinklers x flow from the diagnostics file for that zone.
    • Each zone has a Size: the area from the diagnostics file.
    • Sensor groups say where each value comes from: a weather service, a sensor, a static value, or a mix. The true/false values and the sensors of your diagnostics file tell you what you had.

If you need help, open an issue.

docs.title: Options: the Configure button
docs.text:
Everything is set in the Smart Irrigation panel, in the sidebar. The integration's Configure button (Settings › Devices & services › Smart Irrigation) only says so.

  • The location the weather is read for is Home Assistant's, unless you give other coordinates on the Location coordinates card, under Weather › Weather service. The card shows in advanced mode, or whenever manual coordinates are on. See manual coordinates.
  • The weather service and its API key: see Configuring the weather service.
Coming from 2026.11.0 or earlier

Up to 2026.11.0, Configure asked for manual coordinates, but what it saved was never used: the weather was always read for the coordinates of the panel's card. If you set coordinates there, set them again on the card.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
Export a backup first

Deleting the integration removes its zones, sensor groups, programs and settings. Adding it again starts from nothing, with the setup assistant. If you may want them back, export a backup first under Settings › Backup / restore in the Smart Irrigation panel.

  1. In Settings › Devices & services, open Smart Irrigation, then choose Delete in the three-dot menu.
  2. Remove the files:
    • Installed with HACS: in HACS, find Smart Irrigation and choose Remove in the three-dot menu.
    • Installed by hand: delete the custom_components/smart_irrigation folder.
  3. Restart Home Assistant.

docs.title: To the latest version
docs.text:
• Installed with HACS: HACS, and the Home Assistant updates, show a notification when a new version is out. Install it from there. To check for an update now, use Update information on the repository in HACS.
  • Installed by hand: download the latest release as a zip file and extract it into the custom_components folder of your Home Assistant configuration, over the previous installation.

Then restart Home Assistant.

docs.title: To a specific version
docs.text:
• Installed with HACS: pick the version under Redownload in HACS, or call the update.install action:
    action: update.install
target:
  entity_id: update.smart_irrigation_update
data:
  version: v2026.10.2
  • Installed by hand: download the zip file of the release you want and extract it into the custom_components folder, over the previous installation.

Then restart Home Assistant.

docs.title: Checking the version
docs.text:
• The integration: in Settings › Devices & services › Smart Irrigation, open the hub device. Its firmware version is the installed version.
  • The panel: the version is shown at the top right of the Smart Irrigation panel. If it differs from the integration's, your browser is showing an old copy from its cache: force a refresh.

docs.title: Configuring the weather service
docs.text:
The weather service is set in the Smart Irrigation panel, not when the integration is added. You can turn it on, change it, or turn it off at any time, without reinstalling or reloading anything. Which one to choose is explained on Which weather service.

To set it up:

  1. Open the Smart Irrigation panel from the Home Assistant sidebar.
  2. Go to Weather › Weather service.
  3. Switch on Use a weather service, then pick the service:
    • Open-Meteo (the default) works worldwide and needs no API key.
    • A weather entity in Home Assistant reads one of your weather entities (DWD, Met.no, KNMI...): pick the entity instead of a key. It reports no rain that fell, so each sensor group needs a rain sensor (see weather services).
    • OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather need an API key (see below).
  4. Enter the API key if the service needs one, or pick the weather entity, then Save. The key or the entity is checked before the change is applied, and a message says whether it was accepted.

After switching to a weather entity, the page also names the sensor groups that still take their rain from the weather service: give each of them a rain sensor.

If you turn the weather service off, there is no forecast, and all the weather data must come from your own sensors, set in your sensor groups.

Make sure your Home Assistant location is set correctly so the data matches your garden, or set manual coordinates.

docs.title: Getting an OpenWeatherMap API key
docs.text:
1. Create an account on OpenWeatherMap. Any company name and purpose will do.
  2. Subscribe to the One Call API 3.0 plan. It is a paid plan that is free up to 1000 calls a day, and it must be activated with a payment card. A plain default key is refused.
  3. Copy your key from API keys.

A new key can take a couple of hours to work, as the OpenWeatherMap email says. If you worry about the cost, set a call limit below the paid threshold on the Billing plans page of your profile.

docs.title: Getting a Pirate Weather API key
docs.text: Follow the API Key section of the Pirate Weather documentation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Starting with nothing at all?

Not even Home Assistant? From nothing to a watered garden walks the whole path in half an hour, hardware included, and comes back here for this part.

Smart Irrigation needs Home Assistant 2026.3 or later.

Four steps:

  1. Download the integration from HACS (one click) or by hand, and restart Home Assistant.

  2. Add it in Settings › Devices & services › Add integration › Smart Irrigation. Setup asks nothing: a new Smart Irrigation panel appears in the sidebar.

  3. Turn on a weather service if you want one, under Weather › Weather service in the panel: Open-Meteo is the default and needs no key. Skip this if all your weather comes from your own sensors.

  4. Run the setup assistant (Settings › General, Open the assistant): it asks what Smart Irrigation should do and creates your first zone with its sensor group. From there, configure the rest.

Also in this section:

  • Which weather service to pick, and manual coordinates when the weather should be read somewhere else than your Home Assistant location.
  • Updating to the latest or a specific version.
  • The Configure button on the integration's page, which only points to the panel.
  • Migrating from V1 (v0.0.X), for very old installations.
  • Uninstalling the integration.

docs.title: Assistants (AI)
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation can be offered to an assistant: Claude, ChatGPT or any other client of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or a conversation agent of Home Assistant (Assist). The assistant can then answer questions such as "why was the lawn not watered this morning?", "what will run tomorrow?" or "which zone is the driest?", and set Smart Irrigation up with you: "add a zone for the vegetable garden on the second valve", "water the hedges every other evening".

There is nothing to turn on in Smart Irrigation: it offers itself to Home Assistant (an API of Home Assistant's LLM helper, no server of its own), and no assistant sees it until you pick it there. Whatever it is asked, the assistant never runs a watering and never opens a valve.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• With an MCP client: add Home Assistant's own Model Context Protocol Server integration (Settings › Devices & services › Add integration) and tick Smart Irrigation in its options. Connect the client to Home Assistant as that integration's page explains; Home Assistant does the authentication.
  • With Assist: in the options of your conversation agent, tick Smart Irrigation among the APIs it may use.

Untick it there and the assistant no longer reaches Smart Irrigation.

docs.title: What the assistant can read
docs.text: Tool What it gives GetZones Each zone: state, water balance (mm, a deficit when negative), next duration, valve, size, throughput, lead time, sensor group. GetZoneSettings Every stored setting of one zone (metric). GetIrrigationInfo The next watering and why a zone is held back or skipped, as on the Home tab. GetPrograms The programs, their steps (zones by id and by name) and schedules. GetPlanning What the programs will water over the next days (1 to 14), each run's zones in order and whether the weather is expected to hold it back. GetSensorGroups The sensor groups (where each weather input comes from) and the calculation modules. GetSettings The general settings, in the unit system of Home Assistant, with mode first. FindEntities The valves, switches, sensors and weather entities of Home Assistant, with their unit, device class and the make and model of their device: what the assistant needs to ask you the right questions. PreviewProgram A program as the assistant wrote it, cleaned the way a save cleans it and dry-run on the zones as they are now: each zone's start, end and water, the total, and the zones it could not find. Nothing is saved. GetConfigReference Every field the assistant can write, for a program, its steps, schedules and notifications, and for a zone: type, allowed values or range, unit, default and meaning. The options set only in YAML are flagged yaml_only.

docs.title: What it can change
docs.text:
Tool What it does SaveZone, DeleteZone Create a zone, change its settings, or delete it. SaveSensorGroup, DeleteSensorGroup Create a sensor group, change where its inputs come from, or delete it. SaveSettings Change general settings: mode, what Smart Irrigation does (water, calculate or off: Calculate and water, Calculate only, Stop everything), then calculation, skip conditions, start triggers, sequencing, passes and soak, pumps... The switches mode replaced are refused one by one. SaveProgram, DeleteProgram Add or replace a program, or delete one. A program that names a zone that does not exist is refused.

Every change goes through the path the panel saves with, so the same checks apply: a zone cannot be linked to one of Smart Irrigation's own valves, an unknown setting is refused, a program is cleaned the same way. The assistant is told to say what it is about to change, and most clients ask you before a tool that writes; deleting is marked as such. Each change is written in Home Assistant's log (An assistant saved zone 3, at the info level).

docs.title: Writing a program together
docs.text:
Ask for the program you want ("water the vegetable garden and the greenhouse together every other evening, then the hedges"). The assistant writes it in the YAML shape of the program editor, checks it with PreviewProgram and gives it to you. Paste it under Watering › Programs, with Edit in YAML on a New program or on an existing one: the timeline shows what it would do before you apply it.

The assistant does not have to guess the fields: GetConfigReference lists every one a program, a step, a schedule and a zone can be written with, the YAML-only options included (a step's adjust_seconds, a schedule's months or fallback_time...), with their range and default. So it can set an option the panel's form has no field for, and that no program of yours uses yet.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The assistant receives what these tools return: zone names, entity ids and the names and models of your devices, the weather-based figures and the schedules. With a cloud assistant, that leaves your home. Do not tick Smart Irrigation in the MCP server or the conversation agent if you do not want that.

docs.title: Automations
docs.text:
With Calculate only, Smart Irrigation calculates and something of yours opens the valves: an automation, a blueprint, a controller or another integration. That works with any irrigation system, however it is connected to Home Assistant. (With Calculate and water, Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself, with its programs, and you need none of this.)

Your automation reads the zone's duration sensor, sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name], after it was updated: by the start event, smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones (see events), or after the daily calculation (23:00 by default). Above 0, it is time to water, for that many seconds.

Tell Smart Irrigation the zone was watered

The last step of any watering automation is to call smart_irrigation.credit_watering with how long the zone ran, so the water balance is credited with the water it received. smart_irrigation.set_bucket without a value, which sets the water balance to 0, still works, but loses the deficit a run cut short by the maximum duration did not water.

Resetting the water balance says the soil is at field capacity at that moment, so any rain collected since the last calculation is part of what that statement covers and is not counted again at the next one. Rain falling after the reset still counts as usual. Without that, rain falling between the calculation and the watering would both shorten the run and be counted again in the next water balance.

Deep and infrequent watering is better for most plants: rather than an automation that waters once a week, give the zone an irrigation threshold or set the days between irrigation.

The examples on this page use no timer: see this discussion for an example that uses one for extra safety.

Tip

Writing your own executor rather than using a blueprint? The output contract says exactly what Smart Irrigation publishes, when it changes, and what to send back.

docs.title: Blueprints we provide
docs.text:
A blueprint is a parameterised mould for an automation: you import it once, pick your entities from filtered dropdowns, and Home Assistant writes the automation for you.

You already have them. Smart Irrigation copies the blueprints below into your own blueprints/ folder when it starts, so they are waiting for you under Settings › Automations & scenes › Blueprints, grouped as Smart Irrigation. Nothing to download.

Existing files are never overwritten, so anything you have edited stays yours. That also means an improved blueprint does not reach you on its own: use the Import link in the table below to pull the current version. Each blueprint is copied once: one you delete is not put back at the next start. To copy none at all, switch off Blueprints under Settings › General (advanced mode); the ones already in your folder are left as they are. You can also browse the whole folder.

Pick the one that matches how your valves are actually driven:

Blueprint Use it when standard-irrigation.yaml A plain switch, valve or input_boolean per zone. Turns it on for the calculated duration, then credits the run to the water balance (credit_watering). Has an optional pause switch. Import esphome.yaml An ESPHome device that takes the duration itself. Import simple-scheduler.yaml A script rather than an automation, if you prefer to call irrigation from elsewhere. Import irrigation-unlimited-adjust-time-single-zone.yaml Irrigation Unlimited runs your schedule and you want Smart Irrigation to set the run time of one zone through adjust_time. Import irrigation-unlimited-adjust-time-sequence.yaml The same for one zone inside an IU sequence. Adjusting a sequence as a whole spreads the time across its zones in proportion to their original durations, which is not what a calculated duration means, so this adjusts one zone of it and you add one automation per zone. Import irrigation-unlimited-reset-bucket.yaml Pair with either of the two above: resets the water balance when IU reports the run finished. Import weather-responsive-scheduling.yaml You want a seasonal multiplier applied automatically and runs skipped on cold or windy days. Import valve-watchdog.yaml A backstop: closes a valve left open longer than a limit you set, and tells you. Worth adding whatever else you use. Import rainbird.yaml A Rain Bird controller: starts the Rain Bird zone for the calculated run, in whole minutes. Import hydrawise.yaml A Hunter Hydrawise controller: the same, through hydrawise.start_watering. Import rachio.yaml A Rachio controller: the same, through rachio.start_watering (at most 3 hours a run). Import opensprinkler.yaml An OpenSprinkler controller (the OpenSprinkler integration from HACS): the run in seconds, through opensprinkler.run_station. Import bhyve.yaml An Orbit B-hyve controller (the B-hyve integration from HACS), through bhyve.start_watering. Import

With an off-the-shelf controller (Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler, B-hyve), Smart Irrigation decides how long each zone waters and the controller runs the valves. The off-the-shelf controllers page walks through the setup, which entity to pick for each brand, how to turn off the controller's own schedule, and what to do with several zones. These five have been written against each integration's documented actions but not yet confirmed on real hardware: if you have one, a word on the discussions saying it works, or what it needed, is the most useful contribution there is.

Irrigation-V5 needs no blueprint at all: it reads a numeric entity as a multiplier, so pointing its Adjustment Sensor at our zone sensor with a base watering time of 1 second gives it the calculated duration directly. See executor integration.

With Irrigation Unlimited, note that it exposes binary sensors, not switches: Smart Irrigation tells it how long to run through adjust_time and IU does the running. Do not drive the valve yourself in parallel, or the two will fight.

If you use observed watering (see closed loop), turn off the blueprint's option "Credit the run to the water balance" (the Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler and B-hyve blueprints have it; the standard one always credits, so leave it out): the integration credits the water balance itself and the two would count twice. The ESPHome blueprint, the simple-scheduler script, the Irrigation Unlimited reset blueprint and the example automations below still call set_bucket without a value, which sets the water balance to 0 instead of crediting the run.

docs.title: Example automations
docs.text: The example automations below still call set_bucket without a value at the end. Prefer credit_watering, as above.

docs.title: Example 1: one valve, watering once a week or when the deficit is large
docs.text:
This automation runs daily and checks sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name]. It waters when the water balance is below -25 mm (about 1 inch), or on Mondays when the duration is above 0.

yaml

docs.title: Example 2: one valve, possibly every day
docs.text:
This automation runs when the smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones event fires. If sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] is above 0, it turns on switch.irrigation_tap1, waits that many seconds, and turns it off. Then it resets the water balance with smart_irrigation.set_bucket without a value.

yaml

docs.title: Example 3: one valve, on work days
docs.text:
This automation runs at 05:00, only on the days binary_sensor.workday_sensor allows. As above, it waters switch.irrigation_tap1 for the zone's duration and then resets the water balance. It needs the workday binary sensor, set up separately. You can use a condition on the weekday instead:

condition:
  - condition: time
    weekday:
      - mon
      - thu

yaml

docs.title: Example 4: two valves, on work days
docs.text:
The same at 04:00, for two valves one after the other: switch.irrigation_tap1, then switch.irrigation_tap2, each for its zone's duration, then the water balance is reset. It also needs the workday sensor, or the weekday condition above.

yaml

docs.title: Example 5: six zones on ESPHome
docs.text:
Six zones driven by an ESPHome sprinkler controller. This is the automation the creator of this integration used (ignoring the advice above).

yaml

docs.title: The dashboard card
docs.text: The panel in the sidebar is where an installation is set up, which is occasional work. The card is for the rest of the time: it sits on your dashboard, next to the lights, and says what each zone is short of, how long it would run, and when the water goes on.

docs.title: Adding it
docs.text:
Nothing to install. The integration serves the card and registers it with Lovelace itself, so it is already in the card picker:

  1. Open the dashboard you want it on and press the pencil to edit it.
  2. Add card, then look for Smart Irrigation in the list (searching for "irrigation" finds it).
  3. Set it up in the editor that opens, and save.

If your dashboards are written in YAML, resources are yours to manage and the integration does not touch them. Add this once, under lovelace: resources:, and the log line at startup gives you the exact URL:

resources:
  - url: /api/smart_irrigation/card.js
    type: module

Then put type: custom:smart-irrigation-card in a view.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• The next start, and when a run would be held back, the reason: rain forecast, freeze, wind, rain sensor, days between irrigation, soil moisture, or a postponement.
  • Per zone: the water it is short of, the run that would deliver it, and when it last watered. A zone in manual or disabled state says so next to its name.
  • A zone that would water now is in the accent colour, so a glance is enough.

The deficit is the live estimate, not last night's result. The integration re-runs the same calculation over the readings collected since the zone's last one, without committing anything, and the card shows that with a small icon at the end of the line; hovering it says what the estimate is measured from. A zone calculated minutes ago has nothing new to add, and then the card shows its committed value.

The estimate is computed on the server for every zone, so the card asks for it every two minutes, and not at all while you are looking at another tab or another window. Coming back to it refreshes it at once.

docs.title: The buttons
docs.text: Button What it does Water now (drop) Runs that zone's valve for the calculated duration, and credits the water balance when it finishes. It takes two taps: the first arms it, the second runs it, and it disarms itself after five seconds. It only appears with Calculate and water, for a zone that has a linked valve. Calculate now (calculator) Runs the calculation for that zone now and commits it, as the panel's own button does. Start (play) On a program row: runs the program now, or as soon as it is its turn. Only on an idle program. Pause / Resume On a running or paused program: holds the watering and goes on from where it stopped. Pause calls the global pause_watering service, so it holds all the watering, not one program, and ends by itself after the service's default of 60 minutes if nobody resumes. Next step (skip) Ends the zones of the step in progress and goes on to the next step. Stop (square) Stops the watering and closes the valves. It takes two taps, like Water now.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
With Calculate and water and at least one program, a block above the zones lists one row per program: its name, its state (idle, running, waiting, paused or suspended) and its next start, or the program it starts after. While a program runs, the row shows the step (for example 2/3), the percentage done and the time left. The card asks for this every 5 seconds while a program is running, paused or waiting, and every 60 seconds otherwise, and not at all while the tab is hidden. With Calculate only, or no program, the block is not shown. Hide it with show_programs: false.

Stop acts on all the watering, not on one program.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
All of them are in the visual editor, and this is what they are called in YAML:

Option Default What it does title Smart Irrigation The card's header. zones every zone The zone ids to show. Use it for a card per area, or to keep the greenhouse on its own dashboard. show_next_start true The next start line above the zones. compact false Only the zones that would water now. The card then says "Nothing to water right now" when none would. show_programs true The programs block, shown only with Calculate and water and at least one program. Set it to false to hide it. 
type: custom:smart-irrigation-card
title: Garden
zones: [0, 2]
compact: true

The card speaks the 20 languages of the panel, with English as the fallback.

docs.title: A card from the community
docs.text: Irrigation Zone Card, by @lweberru, is a visual card for one zone at a time: the soil moisture as a ring, the live water balance on a scale with its zero point, the calculated duration, the water used and an optional valve control; the same installation adds Irrigation Overview, a card for the planning, rain and frost protection and the integration-wide actions. It finds a zone's entities from the integration's stable ids, so renamed entities keep working. It is installed from HACS as a custom repository (type Dashboard) and maintained by its author; questions about it go to its repository.

docs.title: Off-the-shelf controllers
docs.text:
If your valves are wired to a commercial controller, you do not have to replace it. Smart Irrigation decides how long each zone waters, and the controller runs the valves, through the action its Home Assistant integration provides. One blueprint per controller does the plumbing:

Controller Integration Action the blueprint calls Unit Longest run Rain Bird Rain Bird (built in) rainbird.start_irrigation minutes 1440 min Hunter Hydrawise Hydrawise (built in) hydrawise.start_watering minutes 1440 min Rachio Rachio (built in) rachio.start_watering minutes 180 min OpenSprinkler hass-opensprinkler (HACS) opensprinkler.run_station seconds 64800 s Orbit B-hyve bhyve-home-assistant (HACS) bhyve.start_watering minutes 1440 min

This is different from Calculate and water, where Smart Irrigation opens and closes a switch or valve entity itself. A controller does not expose its zones that way: you hand it a duration, it starts its own timer and stops on its own. That is what the blueprints do.

Not yet confirmed on real hardware

They were written against each integration's documented actions and their templates are rendered by Home Assistant's own module in our tests, but we do not own the controllers. If you do, a word in the discussions saying it works, or what it needed, is the most useful contribution there is.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Smart Irrigation calculates. At least one zone is in automatic mode and the Home page shows a duration for it after the daily calculation.
  2. Smart Irrigation is on Calculate only, with a start trigger (see start triggers). The blueprints listen to the smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones event; with the trigger on None, that event never fires and nothing waters.
  3. The controller's integration is set up in Home Assistant and its zones show up as entities.
  4. The controller's own schedule is off for the zones Smart Irrigation will drive. Otherwise it waters twice: once on its own program, once on ours. How to do that for each brand is below.

docs.title: Set up one zone
docs.text:
The blueprints are copied into your own blueprints/ folder when the integration starts, so they are already in Home Assistant. If you do not see them, or want the latest version, use the import links on the automations page.

  1. Go to Settings › Automations & scenes › Blueprints and pick Smart Irrigation with Rain Bird (or Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler, B-hyve).
  2. Click Create automation and fill in the three fields:
    • Smart Irrigation zone: the zone's duration sensor, sensor.smart_irrigation_<zone name>. The list only offers Smart Irrigation duration sensors.
    • Controller zone: the entity of the controller zone that waters it. Which entity that is depends on the brand, see the notes below. The list is filtered to that integration.
    • Credit the run to the water balance: leave it on, unless observed watering already watches this controller zone. In that case turn it off, or the run is credited twice.
  3. Save, give the automation the zone's name, and repeat for every zone.

One automation per zone is deliberate: each zone has its own duration and its own water balance.

docs.title: What happens at run time
docs.text:
When the start trigger is reached, every automation created from these blueprints wakes up at the same moment and does the same thing:

  1. Checks the duration. If the zone's duration is 0, nothing happens. On a skipped day the start event is not fired at all, so nothing happens either.
  2. Converts the duration to what the controller takes. Smart Irrigation counts in seconds. Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio and B-hyve take whole minutes, so the run is rounded up (a calculated 3 min 10 s becomes 4 min: a little too much water is better than a deficit left behind) and is at least 1 minute. OpenSprinkler takes seconds and gets them as they are. Every run is capped at the longest run the controller accepts, see the table above. Rachio's cap of 3 hours is the one you may actually hit: if a zone regularly needs more, check its throughput and precipitation rate on the zones page.
  3. Starts the controller zone for that time. The controller runs its own timer and stops the valve itself.
  4. Waits the same time, then credits the run to the water balance of the zone (the credit_watering action, with the time it ran), so the next calculation starts from what the soil really received. A run cut short by the zone's maximum duration keeps the deficit it did not water. If you turned the credit off, the automation just ends.

The automation runs in single mode: a second start event while a run is in progress is ignored.

The controller's own rain sensor or rain delay. If your controller cancels or shortens a run on its own (a wired rain sensor, a rain delay set in the app), the blueprint does not know: it waits the full time and credits the water balance as if the water had gone in. Two ways to keep the books right. Either turn that feature off on the controller and let Smart Irrigation decide, since it already accounts for rain, or use observed watering on the controller zone and turn the blueprint's credit off, so the water balance is credited with what actually ran.

docs.title: Several zones
docs.text:
All the automations start at the same event, so the controller is asked to start every zone at once. What happens next is the controller's business:

  • OpenSprinkler queues the runs and waters the zones one after the other.
  • Rachio and Hydrawise normally run one zone at a time; check in the app what your controller does when a second zone is asked to start while one is running.
  • Rain Bird and B-hyve: same advice, check the app.

If your controller refuses or drops a start while a zone is running, chain the zones yourself. Open the second zone's automation, choose Take control from its menu (the automation stops following the blueprint and becomes editable), and replace its trigger: instead of the start event, trigger on the first controller zone turning off (a state trigger on that entity, from on to off). Keep the actions as they are. Do the same for the third zone on the second, and so on: the zones water in the order you chose, each for its own duration.
