With weather on: only these skip conditions apply (absent: all; postponed always applies).

docs.title: Notify
docs.text: Key Values Default What it does targets list of string notify. (a phone app...) or persistent_notification. None: nothing is stored, nobody is told. when finish, problems finish finish: after every run; problems: only when something went wrong. start boolean false Also tell when a run starts.

docs.title: Being told when a program has watered
docs.text:
Each program has a Notifications section: tick whom to tell, and a summary is sent when the program has watered, one line per zone (minutes and, with a flow meter, litres) and one per problem (a valve that did not open, a run where no water flowed...). The targets are:

  • Notification in Home Assistant: a persistent notification, replaced by the next run of the same program;
  • the notify entities of Home Assistant;
  • the notify actions that are not an entity, such as notify.mobile_app_<phone> of the companion app. On a phone, a run that went wrong comes through with a high priority (Android) and as time-sensitive (iOS), and each program replaces its own previous notification.

When to tell: at the start and at the end of each watering (the start lists the zones about to be watered), only at the end, or only when something goes wrong. A valve that does not close and a pump or main valve that does not do what it is told are told at once, to the program under way, without waiting for the end of the run.

It is off until a target is ticked, and it changes nothing to a run. The events (smart_irrigation_program_finished, smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished...) are still fired, so an automation of your own keeps working beside it. In YAML:

notify:
  targets: [notify.mobile_app_pixel, persistent_notification]
  when: problems        # or finish
  start: false

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A program has any number of schedules, each a moment and the days it applies to.

  • The moment is a time of day, sunrise, sunset, or the moment the sun reaches a bearing (azimuth, in degrees clockwise from north: 90 east, 180 south, 270 west, for a bed the shade of a wall leaves at that moment), with minutes before (-) or after (+). It is either when the program starts or when it must be done. With the second, the start is worked back from the length of what the program has to water (its steps, waits, passes and soaks). A start that has gone by while its moment is still ahead begins at once rather than losing the day, but only after a restart or a reload of Home Assistant, or when its timer was missed. Editing a program, or a calculation that makes the run longer, never starts a run on the spot: an edit at 05:50 of a "done by 06:00" schedule that now needs 20 minutes waits for tomorrow. The same goes for a schedule that starts at its moment: if Home Assistant was down then, the run is caught up after the restart when it is at most 2 hours late and has not run for that occurrence; later than that, it is passed over to the next occurrence.
  • Cut the run at the end time (hard_deadline, only for a schedule that must be done by its moment): by default that moment is a target, and a run that starts late, or has a longer plan than expected, or is paused, simply ends later. Turn it on and the moment is a limit: at that time the zones still open are closed the normal way (each is credited for the water it delivered), the steps not started are dropped, and the program_finished event carries cut: true and reason: "deadline" (the log says so too). A run that gets its turn after the deadline has passed opens nothing. With a deadline, the zones of each step are also ordered driest first (lowest water balance, the largest water deficit); steps keep their order and the zones of a step still open together, so the ordering only decides which zone opens first. If the controller restarts mid-run, the deadline is kept with the run.
  • After a program (type: after): the schedule has no moment of its own and starts its program once another one has finished. See Chaining programs.
  • Polar day and night: a sunrise or sunset schedule has no moment on a day when the sun does not rise or set, and that day is skipped. If there is no sunrise or sunset (fallback_time) chooses what that day does: skip it (the default), use the time of the last sunrise or sunset seen (offset included, looking back at most 60 days; previous), or start at a fixed time (HH:MM). It is YAML only (or set by the services), for instance fallback_time: previous or fallback_time: "06:00" on the schedule (see YAML-only options).
  • Before or after the sun is limited to 12 hours either way (-720 to +720 minutes).
  • The days are filters, and all of them have to hold: they apply to the day of the moment. A run that must be done by Monday 01:00 and takes two hours starts on Sunday at 23:00, and "Monday" is the day that counts. The weather, on the other hand, is judged when the run starts, so that run asks Sunday's conditions. The filters are: days of the week; every N days (N up to 60) with a shift from 0 to N - 1 (three programs with N = 3 and shifts 0, 1 and 2 take turns and never share a day); even or odd days of the month; named days of the month (1, 15, last, where a month too short for a day skips it, 31 in April, and last is every month's own last day); months; and a period of the year, a month and a day picked for each end, which may run over New Year (from November to March; MM-DD in the service, 11-01 to 03-01). The panel's More options of a schedule has the days of the week, every N days and the period. The others are YAML only (or set by the services; see YAML-only options): the shift of every N days (every_offset: 1), even or odd days (parity: even or parity: odd), the days of the month (days_of_month: [1, 15, last]) and the months (months: [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], January is 1).
  • Take the weather into account (weather), a switch, on by default. On, the checks of Weather › Skip watering apply (rain, frost, wind, the days between irrigation, a wet soil, postponed days). What is measured (the rain sensor, the frost, the wind, a postponement) is judged at each start, against what it reads then: a frost at 06:00 holds back a lawn program at 06:00, not a bed program at 18:00 on a mild evening. The rain forecast and the days between irrigation are about the day: they are decided at the first start of the day and kept for the day's later starts, so the morning run, which resets the days since the last irrigation, does not hold back the evening run. On a day when rain is forecast, only the zones the rain cannot reach run. Off is for a greenhouse drip line that does not care (weather: false). In the drawing of a program, the Weather allows it? box gives the answer for its next run: Yes, or No with the check that holds it back (the rain forecast with its millimetres, the wind...). It is left out when no schedule of the program takes the weather into account.
  • Only some of the checks (skip_conditions, YAML only, or set by an assistant, for instance skip_conditions: [rain_sensor, freeze] on the schedule; see YAML-only options): a list choosing which of the skip conditions this schedule applies, among postponed, rain_sensor, freeze, wind, precipitation, days_between and soil_moisture. Left out, all of them apply, as before. Your own postponement always applies when the weather is taken into account. The schedule judges its chosen conditions as every schedule does: what is measured at the moment it starts, the rain forecast and the days between irrigation from the day's decision (made at the day's first start, whatever conditions that start chose); the holds that follow (days between per zone, a moist soil, rain since the calculation) are the same ones, except that a zone is only held by its days between when that condition is chosen, and by a moist soil only when soil_moisture is chosen. Those holds change the zones' durations for the whole day, so they cannot be undone: if a schedule that applies the moist soil hold ran first, a later schedule of the same day that left soil_moisture out finds those zones already at zero. The other way round works: a schedule that left it out first does not stop a later one from applying it. Switching the schedule's weather off in the panel keeps the list but it no longer applies; switched on again, it applies again.

Good to know: the weather holds work on the zones' calculated durations, which all programs share. On a day a weather-aware start has held a zone back, a program that ignores the weather but waters that zone for its calculated duration finds nothing to water. For a zone that must be watered whatever the weather says, give its step a fixed duration.

A schedule that comes due while its program is already running or waiting starts nothing and counts no watering day; the days between irrigations are only reset for the zones that really start. A program deleted or suspended while it runs stops before its next step. Deleting a program or a schedule also clears what was remembered of its last run, so a new schedule never inherits it.

An occurrence counts as fired as soon as it comes due, whatever happens next: a schedule that is suspended, whose program is already running, or that the weather holds back is not tried again for that occurrence. A scheduled run that is waiting for its turn when Home Assistant restarts is not kept (only a queued manual run is, see below): it is lost until the schedule's next occurrence.

The Smart Irrigation schedules are armed when a setting changes, after a calculation and at a new day, like the start trigger.

The length a "must be done" schedule works back from is the one the Planning chart and the program sensors show, with the adjust_program adjustment in force included. Setting or clearing an adjustment arms the schedules again at once, so the start moves with it.

docs.title: Chaining programs
docs.text:
A schedule can start its program after another program, the way backup jobs are chained: "water the beds 10 minutes after the lawn is done". The second program follows the first whatever its length, which changes every day with the weather, so there is no start time to guess and no gap or overlap to fix by hand.

What it is for:

  • One after the other on the same water: the beds after the lawn on the same well, pump or tank, with a pause in between so the well or the tank fills up again (offset_minutes: 30).
  • Something that only makes sense after a watering: a fertiliser program, a line flush, the pots on the terrace on Saturdays only.
  • Programs with their own rules in one sequence: each one keeps its own steps, days and weather, and a third program can follow the second.

In the schedule, set When to After a program, pick the program in Program, and in Minutes after it ends how long to wait once it has finished (0, right away, up to 720; never before). That moment is when the program stays on starts: the end of a run still to come cannot be aimed at, so hard_deadline does not apply either. In YAML:

name: Beds
steps:
  - zones: [Beds, Hedge]
schedules:
  - type: after
    after_program: Lawn
    offset_minutes: 30
    weekdays: [5]                           # Saturdays only (0 is Monday)

The rules:

  • When the other program really watered (it went to its end, or was cut by its deadline, and at least one zone got water), it starts once that one has finished, plus the offset, whether the other was started by its own schedule or with Run now.
  • When a scheduled run of the other program did not water because it was held back (by the weather, a suspension, or nothing to water), it still starts, at that run's planned moment plus the offset (for a "must be done by" schedule, that moment is its end). Its own weather setting decides then: a greenhouse drip line with the weather off, chained after a lawn program held back by a frost, waters all the same; one that takes the weather into account is judged by it, and the frost holds it back too. A chain of chains passes the moment on: when the second program is held back as well, the third starts at the second one's moment plus its own offset.
  • It does not start when the other program was stopped (Stop, stop_watering, stop_program, a run that replaced it, or the program deleted, suspended or Smart Irrigation switched off while it ran): whoever stopped the watering did not want the next program either. Nor when the other run failed (no zone got water because its valves did not open, or its deadline had passed before its turn): something is wrong, and it is for you to look at. Nor when the other program was already running when its schedule came (its run under way starts what comes after it when it ends), nor when Smart Irrigation is switched off or calculates only. A manual Run now that finds nothing to water starts nothing after it.
  • Then it is a start like any other: its own days are judged on the day it would start (a run that ends at 23:50 with a 20 minute offset is judged on the next day), its own weather is judged when it starts, it takes its turn on its supplies, and it starts nothing when its program is suspended or already running. Its own finish can start a third program in turn.
  • Programs cannot start after each other in a loop (A after B after A, or A after itself): the save is refused, and the program list does not offer the program that would close it. A program another one starts after cannot be deleted (the schedule waits for it, switched on or not): Delete the program is greyed out with the reason, until that schedule is changed. A schedule that still waits for a program that is gone (an old backup) says so and never starts.
  • A start waiting for its offset is recorded and survives a restart: one that came due while Home Assistant was down starts late when it is at most 2 hours late, and is given up beyond. A newer finish of the same program (run again by hand during the wait) replaces it.
  • The planning, the week view and the flow place it right after the planned end of the other program, plus the offset, on the days its filters allow. After a run of that program that is not expected to water (the forecast holds it back, it is suspended, or it has nothing to water), it is placed at that run's planned moment plus the offset instead. Nothing is planned when that program is not planned in the window.

docs.title: Irrigate all zones now
docs.text: The Irrigate all zones button of the hub device runs every zone that has a valve once, as a one-off: it is not a program and has no schedule. Its order (one after the other or all at once), its passes and its pause between zones are under Watering › Programs, folded at the bottom of the card under Settings of the Irrigate all zones button, in advanced mode (the block shows in every mode once one of them is changed: all at once, more than one pass or a pause). They change nothing to the programs, which water their own steps. The run takes its turn on every supply, fires smart_irrigation_irrigation_started and smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished, and credits each zone for what it delivered.

docs.title: Driving the watering
docs.text:
The Programs card: each program's header row has its actions as icons, beside its name and its state (running, paused or waiting for its turn, with the step and the time left): Run now, Stop this program while it is under way, Edit in YAML, and the Options for this run (a total duration, and whether to replace what is running) for the next press of Run now. Pause, Next step and Stop for everything that is watering are on the Home page, while something waters. And these services:

Service What it does smart_irrigation.run_program Runs a program now, or when it is its turn. Optional seconds (1 to 86400) is a total for the whole program, shared between its steps in proportion to their planned durations; left out, the planned durations. A program that is already running or waiting, or suspended, is not run, with a line in the log. A program whose schedules are all off runs all the same: they only decide when it starts on its own. Optional mode: queue (default) takes the turn behind what is running, replace first stops what runs and waits, cleanly (valves closed, delivered water credited), then runs the program. smart_irrigation.water_zone Waters a zone for a number of seconds of water, or for its calculated duration. With mode: queue (default) it takes its turn like everything else; with mode: replace it first stops what is running and waiting. With several zones, only the first replaces, the others follow it. A zone you suspended is watered anyway: asking for it by hand overrides the suspension. smart_irrigation.stop_program Stops one program: if it runs, its open zones close the normal way and are credited for what they delivered, and no further step starts; if it waits for its turn, it is taken out of the queue. An unknown id does nothing. smart_irrigation.set_step_enabled, set_schedule_enabled Switch one of a program's steps (step_id) or one of its schedules (schedule_id) on or off (enabled), as the panel does (set_program_enabled is deprecated): the schedules are armed again and the panel refreshes. With Calculate only nothing changes; an unknown program, step or schedule id is refused with an error. smart_irrigation.pause_watering Closes the open valves and holds everything, the zones waiting included. The clock stops: what was delivered is credited and, after the resume, the part of the pass still owed is watered. A pause that is not lifted ends by itself after an hour (or the minutes given). smart_irrigation.resume_watering Goes on from where the pause stopped. smart_irrigation.next_step Ends the zones of the step a program is on, and lets it go on. With overlapping steps, it ends every step that is open. Programs on supplies of their own water side by side: program_id moves only that one on, and without it every program that is running moves on. smart_irrigation.stop_watering Stops now: every valve is closed, each zone is credited for the water it delivered, programs and waiting zones end. With zones chosen, only those, and the programs under way or waiting do not water those zones in their later steps either. Without zones it also ends a pause. smart_irrigation.suspend Keeps a zone or a program from watering for some hours or until a date. Zero hours lifts it. Hours are limited to 8760, a date that cannot be read is refused (it never lifts a suspension), and an unknown program id is ignored. smart_irrigation.adjust_program Makes a program water longer or shorter for a while (Irrigation Unlimited's adjust_time): a percent (0 to 1000) of every step's water, and/or seconds added to it, for hours (1 to 8760) or until reset. It replaces the previous adjustment instead of adding to it, applies to the runs that start after it is set (not to the one under way), survives a restart, and reset: true clears it. Refused with Calculate only, and for an unknown program id. The program's sensor shows it in the adjustment attribute. smart_irrigation.use_measured_throughput Takes the flow a zone's meter measured as its throughput. The measurement is advice and is never applied on its own.

docs.title: Seeing what is going on
docs.text:
• The Planning page draws what the programs will water over the next days (3, 7 or 14) as a chart: hover a run for its zones and minutes, why the weather may hold it back, and what it waits for or starts after; a click opens its program. Under it, the Watering now card shows what is watering now: the step, the round, how far along, the valves that are open and for how much longer. Each planned run carries its expected seconds. For a run in the next 48 hours (as far as the rain forecast reaches) it also says when the forecast would hold it back: skipped_reason is precipitation, with the forecast and threshold behind it. A run that ignores the weather, or one further away, gets no reason: the weather is not known days ahead, and a planned run goes ahead if nothing holds it back. Only forecast conditions are predicted, not what the sensors read now. The planning lists the schedules that are on, and ignores suspensions and postponements: a suspended program still appears. For each run, steps lists the zones of the first round only, while expected_seconds covers all the rounds. The data also carries forecast_known (whether a forecast could be read) and sheltered_zone_ids (the zones that still run on a day the rain holds back), but the panel shows only the forecast rain (forecast_mm).
  • A dry zone nothing will water. Once a day, an automatic zone whose water balance has been dry for more than 3 days while no program covers it raises a repair notice (one per zone) and fires smart_irrigation_zone_unwatered. Dry means a deficit of at least half the zone's maximum water balance, or its irrigation threshold when that is larger (never under 1 mm). Covered means a program that is not suspended has an enabled schedule and an enabled step with the zone. A zone you suspended yourself is left alone. The notice clears when the zone is watered or a program covers it again. The count of dry days starts again after a restart or after any reload of the integration. The check also runs at once whenever the programs are changed, so a zone that a new program covers stops being a candidate straight away.
  • One sensor per program (sensor.smart_irrigation_program_<id>): idle, waiting, running, paused or suspended, with the next start, the last run, the suspension and, while it runs, the step and how far along. See entities for the attributes.
  • A check while a valve is open. Every 60 seconds, the zone's linked valve is read. If it reads off, closed or closing, it shut by itself (a water-shortage auto-close, a timed-off that ran out, somebody closing it at the device): smart_irrigation_valve_out_of_sync is fired, with a smart_irrigation_zone_problem of reason valve_closed_early, and the zone's run ends. The valve is not opened again, so a device that closed for lack of water stays shut. The zone is credited for the time the valve was open, taken from the moment its state changed (or, failing that, the moment the check noticed it, so the credit is then exact to about a minute). A valve that reads unknown or unavailable is never taken for a closed one. Only the linked valve is checked, not the extra ones.
  • Events. The other events keep firing too.
    • smart_irrigation_program_started: program_id, program (the name), manual, tours (the rounds), zones (the first round only, each {zone_id, zone, seconds}) and resumed: true when the run goes on after a restart.
    • smart_irrigation_program_finished: program_id, program, manual, zones (what was watered, with seconds, volume_l and the new water balance), problems ({zone_id, zone, reason}) and stopped. A program that starts after this one starts when zones is not empty and stopped is false, or cut is true (or, after a scheduled run held back or with nothing to water, at that run's planned moment). A run cut at its deadline adds cut: true and reason: "deadline". It is not fired for a plan with nothing to water, nor for a run taken out of the queue before its turn. A run whose deadline has already passed when its turn comes fires program_finished (cut) and no program_started.
    • smart_irrigation_valve_on and smart_irrigation_valve_off, at every switch of a valve or a supply: entity_id, kind (zone or supply) and, for a zone, zone_id and zone, for a supply supply_id and supply. The off of a zone valve adds closed (whether it really closed).
    • smart_irrigation_valve_out_of_sync: zone_id, zone, entity_id, expected (open), actual and reason (closed_early).
    • smart_irrigation_supply_problem: supply_id, supply, entity_id and reason, as above.

docs.title: When Home Assistant restarts
docs.text:
A program run and a cycle that is under way are recorded as they go. After a restart the run that was open is finished from its own record first, then the steps still to do follow, one at a time. Programs that were watering side by side each have their own record and each go on with their own steps. A run more than six hours old is not resumed: it belongs to another day. With overlapping steps, the record is that of the later step: the earlier one that was still open is finished from its own record, and the later one restarts with the zones it had not started. What is not resumed: the remaining passes of the zone that was open (only the pass in progress is).

A pause survives a restart while its end is still ahead: the watering is held again until then (or until you resume), and the valves that were open are not reopened by the pause itself; the program goes on from the resume as it does after any pause. A valve run interrupted by the restart is held the same way: nothing is opened (the pump included) while the pause lasts, and the rest of its pass is watered after the resume, with the water delivered before the restart credited once. A manual run you stopped while it waited is also removed from the stored queue at once, and queued runs wait for every run resumed after the restart (a valve run or a cycle, not only a program) before they start. The water a pause owes is kept too: when a pause closes the valves of a step, what each zone still owes (and the passes after it) is recorded, so a reload (an options save) or a restart during the pause does not lose it. After it, and once the pause is over, those zones water what they owed first (credited once, the part delivered before the pause having been credited already), then the program goes on with the next steps. A pause that ended while Home Assistant was down is not held again, and the owed water is watered at once; owed water more than 30 hours old is dropped. Manual runs waiting for their turn (a run_program asked for during another program) are kept too: after a restart they are put back in line, behind a program that is being resumed, unless they are more than six hours old or their program is gone, disabled or suspended.

A valve that is slow to say it is open, a battery valve on Zigbee for instance, is given 30 seconds and is asked to open again at 10 and 20 seconds. Only one that stays closed after that is a failure, reported as valve_did_not_open. A zone can set its own wait (advanced mode) and number of resends (open_resends, YAML only), for a cloud valve that confirms slowly or should not be asked twice: see the confirmation per zone.

A Sonoff SWV on ZHA is opened with one command that also starts its own timer, so it closes itself even if Home Assistant dies right after opening it. See hardware auto-off for the details and the other valves.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: • A flow meter shared by zones that water at the same time cannot tell their water apart. While they overlap, their volume limit counts the meter's litres divided equally by the number of zones on it (an approximation), and their litres are not credited from the meter nor used to calibrate the measured flow: they are credited by time, and a line in the log says so once. Give each zone its own meter for exact limits and calibration.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: It is not a pressure controller, a master-valve scheduler for a whole farm, or a replacement for a controller that already does its job. If a Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler or B-hyve runs your valves, its blueprint is the right way, with Calculate only, and the programs have nothing to add to it.

docs.title: Info and history
docs.text: The Home tab answers the questions the other tabs cannot: what is about to happen, and what already happened. Info is its first page, History its second.

docs.title: One answer, first
docs.text:
The page opens with a single sentence: this zone will water for so long at the next start, or nothing is short of water, or a postponement is holding it back, or the weather is. While something waters, it says Watering now, with Pause, Next step and Stop at hand.

Underneath it, the detail: what decides the start, whether it works back from sunrise, the zones that would run and how the total is counted. When the start works back from sunrise, it is the moment the run has to begin to finish on time, so it moves with the season and with the durations themselves. A run shortened by rain still starts when it was scheduled and finishes early, rather than starting late.

Three warnings stand above the sentence while they are true, since each needs something done:

  • Nothing is armed to start a run that is owed. The time shown is arithmetic; whether anything is armed to act on it is another question.
  • A zone is no longer being calculated, with the date of its last calculation. One zone can freeze while everything else works, and it then waters on the weather of days ago.
  • This installation would never water, when the configuration says so: No watering duration is being calculated, No zone waters on its own, or Nothing here opens a valve. An installation can be correct, update its durations every night and never open a valve, in silence: this says so.

Everything else comes after the sentence, the buttons to hold watering back first.

docs.title: Hold watering back
docs.text: Hold for 24 h and Hold for 48 h postpone every zone, for rain the forecast missed or an afternoon on the lawn; Resume now lifts it. A postponement ends by itself and resets nothing, so the deficit it held back is still there afterwards. The same thing is available as the postpone_irrigation and resume_irrigation actions, and as buttons of the hub device (see entities).

docs.title: Will it be skipped?
docs.text:
When nothing holds the next run back, the card says so in one line; open it for the checks. When something does, the checks are shown straight away.

Seven checks can hold a run back, each with its own state and its own numbers: a postponement of yours, the rain sensor, the freeze, the wind, the rain forecast against your threshold, the days since the last watering against the days between irrigation, and the soil moisture of the zones. They are set on Weather › Skip watering.

This is a preview, not a promise. It is evaluated now, and a forecast can change before the start. That is also why a projected skip does not move the next start to the following day: the page says the start would be skipped on the forecast as it stands, and shows the numbers it says it from.

Underneath, the last real decision, with the moment it was taken.

To be told rather than to look, use the smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped event, fired when a start is skipped, with the reason.

docs.title: Where each zone stands
docs.text:
For every zone: the deficit now, the deficit at its last calculation, how long it would water if it ran at this moment, and when it last watered.

The headline and this table use the live estimate. With the watering duration set to Just before each start, the announced run is the estimate, and a line says so. The warning No watering duration is being calculated only appears when the watering duration is set to Only when I ask (see General settings). With Calculate only and the active start trigger on None, the page says No trigger is active. At last calculation shows the day and time of that calculation.

"Now" is an estimate. It re-runs the calculation over the readings collected since the last one and throws the result away: nothing is written, no reading is consumed, and the zone keeps the value of its last calculation until the next one. It is there to answer "what would happen if it ran right now" without disturbing anything.

A zone shows nothing here when no reading has arrived since it last calculated, which is normal in the minutes after a calculation.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The History page lists what actually ran, grouped by day: which zone, when, for how long and how much water. A run appears whether Smart Irrigation drove the valve itself or observed one being driven by something else.

The Weather › Weather service page keeps its own history of what was retrieved and when, which is the place to look when a calculation used a value you did not expect.

For the full chain behind a single number, from each raw reading to the duration, there is the opt-in calculation log.

docs.title: The output contract
docs.text:
This page is for anybody who drives the water themselves, with Calculate only: your own automation, a controller integration, or another integration that wants to consume what Smart Irrigation decides. It is one page on purpose, so it can be read without reading the rest, and it says what is promised and what is not. See also entities, events and automations.

Smart Irrigation calculates. Something else opens a valve. This is the interface between the two.

docs.title: The one number
docs.text:
Per zone, one sensor carries the answer:

sensor.smart_irrigation_<zone name>
  • The state is a number of whole seconds. It is the time that zone needs the water on for.
  • 0 means do nothing. Not "run briefly": there is nothing owed, or what is owed is below the zone's threshold, so a run would be a trickle. Treat 0 as a skip.
  • It is never negative.
  • Its attributes carry the rest (the water balance, the water need, the units in use, the last calculation): see entities.

How that number is produced, in order: the soil water deficit in millimetres, divided by the zone's precipitation rate, gives an hour fraction; that becomes seconds. Below the zone's irrigation threshold the result is 0. Above the zone's maximum duration the result is that maximum. The zone's lead time is then added, and the whole is rounded to the second, so a zone with a lead time can publish slightly more than its maximum duration: the maximum bounds the watering, the lead time is the delay before water actually arrives.

The crop factor is not applied here. It scales the evapotranspiration that lowers the water balance, so the deficit already carries it.

docs.title: When it changes
docs.text:
1. At the calculation time (23:00 by default, or a schedule of your own, or the calculate action). Every automatic zone gets a new duration.
  2. At the start trigger, just before the start event fires: rain that fell between the calculation and now shortens the run, zones sheltered from forecast rain are separated from exposed ones, and a zone whose own soil moisture sensor says it is wet is held back. So the duration you read when the event arrives is the one to use, not the one from the night.
  3. After a run is credited, if you use observed watering or Calculate and water: crediting the water balance recomputes the duration from it, which normally lands on 0.
  4. Never on its own between those. The number stands until one of the above.

If you want a value that moves with the weather through the day, that is the Live water balance sensor, which is an estimate and is documented as one.

docs.title: The events
docs.text:
Event When Data smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones A start trigger is reached and today is a watering day The trigger's identity smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped A start trigger is reached and today is not The trigger's identity, reason, and checks, the same detail the Home page shows smart_irrigation_irrigation_started Smart Irrigation begins a run (Calculate and water) sequencing, and zones: {zone_id, zone, seconds} smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished Smart Irrigation finishes a run (Calculate and water) zones: {zone_id, zone, seconds, volume_l, bucket}, and problems: {zone_id, zone, reason} smart_irrigation_zone_problem A valve Smart Irrigation drives did not open, did not close, or opened with no water flowing zone_id, zone, entity_id, reason (valve_did_not_open, valve_did_not_close, no_flow, valve_closed_early, supply_did_not_turn_on, valve_timer_not_set) smart_irrigation_program_started Calculate and water: a program run begins program_id, program, manual, tours, zones (first round only: {zone_id, zone, seconds}), and resumed after a restart smart_irrigation_program_finished Calculate and water: a program run ends program_id, program, manual, zones, problems, stopped, and cut and reason (deadline) when the run was cut smart_irrigation_valve_on / smart_irrigation_valve_off Calculate and water: a zone valve or a supply is switched entity_id, kind (zone or supply), zone_id and zone or supply_id and supply; the off of a zone valve adds closed smart_irrigation_supply_problem Calculate and water: a pump or main valve did not come on or go off supply_id, supply, entity_id, reason (supply_did_not_turn_on, supply_did_not_turn_off) smart_irrigation_valve_out_of_sync Calculate and water: a valve held open reads closed (checked every 60 seconds); it is not opened again zone_id, zone, entity_id, expected (open), actual (off, closed...), reason (closed_early) smart_irrigation_weather_stale A temperature, humidity, dew point, wind speed or pressure source of a sensor group has not reported for 6 hours; fired once per silence mapping_id, mapping, fields (the fields that just went silent), since (ISO time of the last report) smart_irrigation_weather_recovered Fields that were silent report again, or the outage stops being watched mapping_id, mapping, fields, reason (unloaded or unwatched, absent on a real recovery) smart_irrigation_zone_unwatered Calculate and water: a zone has been dry for over 3 days and no program will water it; fired once, with a repair notice zone_id, zone, days, deficit_mm

The skip event exists because the absence of an event is not something an automation can listen for.

docs.title: Consuming it
docs.text:
As seconds. Read the sensor, open the valve, wait that long, close it. This is what the standard-irrigation blueprint does.

As minutes. Most off-the-shelf controllers take whole minutes. Round up, never down: rounding 90 seconds down to one minute loses a third of the water, and the deficit then rolls to the next day. The controller blueprints do this.

As a percentage or a coefficient. Some schedulers do not take a duration, they scale their own base time. Ours is an absolute need, not a scaling of somebody's schedule, so the mapping has to be made explicit:

  • with a base time of 1 second, a multiplier-based system reads the seconds directly. That is why Irrigation-V5 needs no blueprint: point its adjustment sensor at the zone sensor and set the base watering time to 1 second.
  • with a real base time, the percentage is our seconds / base seconds x 100, and the scheduler's own limits apply.
  • Irrigation Unlimited takes both: adjust_time in actual mode takes a duration, which is what our blueprints use. Adjusting a sequence rather than a zone spreads the time across its zones in proportion to their original durations, which is not what a calculated duration means, so adjust one zone at a time.

docs.title: What to send back
docs.text:
In open loop, tell us how long the zone ran, or the deficit stays and the zone waters again tomorrow:

action: smart_irrigation.credit_watering
target:
  entity_id: sensor.smart_irrigation_lawn
data:
  seconds: 900

Leave seconds out and the zone's own duration is credited. This credits the water the run put down, where set_bucket without a value sets the water balance to 0 whatever it did: a run cut short by the zone's maximum duration then lost the deficit it had not watered. set_bucket without a value still works, and is right when you want to say the soil is at field capacity.

In closed loop (observed watering or Calculate and water), send nothing: the integration credits the water balance from the run itself. Calling credit_watering or set_bucket as well counts the water twice, which pushes the water balance too high and makes the next calculation ask for less than it should.

Never both, and never a blueprint that resets the water balance on top of a closed-loop setup. The closed loop page says which is which.

docs.title: Promised, and not promised
docs.text:
Promised.

  • The duration is whole seconds, 0 or positive, one per zone.
  • 0 means no run at all.
  • Depths in the entities follow Home Assistant's unit system; internally everything is metric and converted at the edges only.
  • The start event fires once per trigger, and either it or the skip event fires when a trigger is reached.
  • The duration published when the start event fires already accounts for rain since the calculation.
  • The zone sensors never carry a runtime adjustment. With Calculate and water, smart_irrigation.adjust_program changes how long a program's steps water (a percentage and/or seconds, for a while); it is applied by the controller to the runs it starts, and shown in the adjustment attribute of the program's sensor, not in the zone's number.
  • Its run actions leave the zone's number alone too: run_program and water_zone take an optional seconds and a mode (queue, the default, or replace), stop_program ends one program, and set_step_enabled and set_schedule_enabled switch a step or a schedule on or off (set_program_enabled is deprecated, see no main program). See driving the watering.

Not promised.

  • That a zone has a duration at all: a zone with no precipitation rate (no area and flow, no rate) cannot have one, and publishes 0.
  • That the run finishes before any particular moment. The default trigger works back from sunrise using the sum or the maximum of the zone durations depending on the sequencing, plus soaking and pauses when Smart Irrigation performs the run, but nothing here can know how long your own executor takes.
  • That the number will not change between the event and your action: an executor that waits an hour before starting should read the sensor again.
  • That a zone's duration is independent of the others. The sequencing setting decides what the whole run is taken to be.

docs.title: If you maintain an integration
docs.text: If you want to consume this from another integration rather than from an automation, the same contract applies and the events above are the hook. The zone entities are stable: the duration sensor's entity_id and its recorded history have been preserved across every version of this integration, deliberately. An issue or a discussion is the place to ask for something the contract does not cover yet.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation adds these actions (services) to Home Assistant. Where an action acts on zones, a target picks them, and no target means every zone. A zone is picked by its sensor (sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone]); picking an area or a device is refused, so it never stands for every zone. The services that deal with the water balance keep ids with bucket in them, such as smart_irrigation.set_bucket.

Service Description smart_irrigation.calculate Calculates the zones picked, or every automatic zone when none is picked. Weather data used is deleted afterwards unless you specify delete_weather_data: false. Specify dry_run: true to see what the calculation would do without changing anything: see Dry run below. smart_irrigation.update_weather Fetches the weather for the zones picked, or for every automatic zone when none is picked. smart_irrigation.clear_all_weather_data Deletes all weather data. Pick zones and only the weather data of their sensor groups is deleted (the other zones of those groups lose it too, since a group's data is shared). smart_irrigation.generate_watering_calendar Generates a 12-month watering calendar for a zone based on representative climate data. smart_irrigation.credit_watering Credits a zone with the water a run of your own delivered: its precipitation rate times seconds (the zone's duration when left out), less its lead time. Use it at the end of an irrigation automation rather than resetting the water balance: a run cut short by the zone's maximum duration keeps the deficit it did not water. smart_irrigation.set_bucket Sets the water balance of the zones picked, or of every zone when none is picked, to new_bucket_value. Without a value it is 0, the reset: the soil back at field capacity, whatever the run delivered, so credit_watering is the better end to an irrigation automation. smart_irrigation.set_multiplier Sets the crop factor (multiplier) of the zones picked, or of every zone when none is picked, to new_multiplier_value (required; the form suggests 1.0). smart_irrigation.set_zone Sets a zone's water balance (new_bucket_value, default 0), crop factor (new_multiplier_value, default 1.0), duration (new_duration_value, default 0), state (new_state_value, default automatic) and throughput (new_throughput_value, default 50). smart_irrigation.postpone_irrigation Holds watering back for hours (default 24), for rain the forecast missed or an afternoon on the lawn. It is a moment, not a countdown: it survives a restart and ends by itself. It resets nothing, so a zone that is short of water still is when it ends. hours: 0 lifts it. smart_irrigation.resume_irrigation Lifts a postponement now. smart_irrigation.set_seasonal_adjustment Scales the crop factor, and shifts the irrigation threshold, over a range of months. Without adjustment_id it creates an adjustment; with it, it changes that one, and with remove: true as well it removes it. smart_irrigation.use_measured_throughput Sets a zone's throughput to the flow its water meter measured over its runs. The measurement is advice, never applied on its own: this is how to accept it. smart_irrigation.run_program, water_zone, pause_watering, resume_watering, next_step, stop_watering, stop_program, suspend, adjust_program, set_step_enabled, set_schedule_enabled Drive the watering with Calculate and water (see driving the watering): run a program or a zone now, pause, skip a step, stop, make a program water longer or shorter for a while, or set a zone or a program aside. suspend refuses an until more than 8760 hours (a year) ahead. set_program_enabled is deprecated (removed in 2027.11): use set_schedule_enabled.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
calculate accepts dry_run: true. A dry run computes the result and returns it without touching any of your irrigation data: the water balance, the zone, the collected weather data and the internal "last calculated" marker are all left exactly as they were.

Use it when you want to inspect a zone during the day without disturbing the scheduled calculation. A normal manual calculation consumes the weather data collected so far and moves the internal "last calculated" marker, which means the scheduled run later that day only sees a partial window. Evapotranspiration is computed as a full-day rate from that window and then scaled by its length, and because the minimum and maximum temperature are taken from the samples inside the window, a partial window never contains the full daily temperature swing. The result is a lower daily total than if the scheduled run had seen the whole day. A dry run avoids this entirely.

One thing a dry run does still do: if your zone is calculated by Smart Irrigation with Look ahead (forecast_days) above 0, it fetches forecast data from your weather service just like a real calculation, because the preview has to be computed from the same inputs to be meaningful. Subject to the usual cache, that can count against your weather service's API quota, so avoid polling a dry run in a tight loop.

Because a dry run stores nothing, the outcome is only available as the service response:

action: smart_irrigation.calculate
target:
  entity_id: sensor.smart_irrigation_my_zone
data:
  dry_run: true
response_variable: result

result.zones then holds the delta, bucket, duration, current_drainage and et_deficiency the calculation would have produced for each zone. All five keys are always present, and are null when the zone's module does not produce that value. Zones that produced no result at all are left out of the list entirely.

docs.title: Actions on their way out
docs.text:
Until 2026.11 there were pairs of actions for one zone and for all zones. They became one action each, and the recurring schedules gave way to the programs' schedules. The old names keep working until version 2027.11 at the earliest, and are removed in winter, outside the watering season. Each call to one logs a warning and raises a repair issue that says what to use instead.

Old action Use instead calculate_zone, calculate_all_zones calculate, with the zones as target or none for all update_zone, update_all_zones update_weather, the same way reset_bucket, reset_all_buckets set_bucket without a value (it is 0), with the zones or none for all set_all_buckets set_bucket without a target set_all_multipliers set_multiplier without a target create_seasonal_adjustment, update_seasonal_adjustment, delete_seasonal_adjustment set_seasonal_adjustment: no adjustment_id creates, an id changes, an id with remove: true removes create_recurring_schedule, update_recurring_schedule, delete_recurring_schedule The programs' schedules, under Watering › Programs (Calculate and water). No action replaces these.

The blueprints we ship call the new names. A blueprint Smart Irrigation laid down and you never edited is replaced by the new version when Home Assistant starts; one you edited is left as it is, and keeps working on the old name until then.

docs.title: Nothing ever waters
docs.text:
The Home page answers first: it says whether the installation would ever water, and names the reason when it would not (see Info). Then check what Settings › General says Smart Irrigation does:

  • Calculate and water: a zone is only watered once a program has it in a step, and only when it has a Linked valve/switch. Watering › Planning shows what will run.
  • Calculate only: Smart Irrigation opens no valve. Your automation, blueprint or controller does, on the start event of the active start trigger. With the trigger on None, nothing starts.
  • Stop everything: nothing is calculated or watered.

docs.title: The diagnostics file
docs.text: To get help, a diagnostics file is the most useful thing to attach to an issue. In Settings › Devices & services › Smart Irrigation (or this link), choose Download diagnostics in the three-dot menu. The storage file, smart_irrigation.storage in the .storage folder of your configuration, holds the same configuration.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
The file is JSON. It lists your settings, zones, sensor groups and modules, and the weather data collected. The weather data is stored in metric, so it may not match what the panel shows:

  • dew point, temperature: degrees Celsius (°C);
  • evapotranspiration, total precipitation: millimetres (mm);
  • humidity: percent (%);
  • pressure: hectopascals (hPa), converted to absolute pressure when provided as relative;
  • solar radiation: megajoules per square metre per day (MJ/day/m²);
  • wind speed: metres per second (m/s).

These are the units the FAO-56 calculation works in. Most of the conversions are in helpers.py.

docs.title: "A zone is never watered and its deficit does not move"
docs.text:
When every day of the window lacks something the equation needs (a temperature, the wind), the evapotranspiration comes out as nothing: the deficit stays where it was and the zone is never watered, which looks exactly like a zone with no need. Smart Irrigation now raises a repair issue naming the zone and the inputs that were missing, and clears it at the next calculation that can be done. Check that the sensors mapped to those fields are available, or that the weather service still sends them.

A repair issue also appears when one run of a zone cannot water what the zone loses between two waterings (see Maximum duration in the zone settings).

docs.title: A zone says it cannot be calculated
docs.text:
When the calculation of an automatic zone fails, the zone keeps its last water balance and is not watered. Smart Irrigation says so in three places until a calculation succeeds: the zone's line in the Zones tab (red, with the reason, instead of "nothing to water"), the zone's problem sensor (binary_sensor.smart_irrigation_<zone>_problem, on, with the reason in its reason and calculation attributes), and a repair notice. The reasons and what to do:

  • No sensor group: a zone added on the Zones tab has none until one is chosen. Choose it on the zone's card.
  • No weather readings: the zone's sensor group has no readings. Check that it has sources and that they report, update the weather data, then calculate the zone.
  • No module: choose how the zone is calculated on its card.
  • No evapotranspiration: the zone takes its evapotranspiration from a sensor or a weather service, and the sensor group had none. Check that sensor or the service.
  • A forecast without a weather service: the zone looks days ahead, which needs a weather service. Set one up, or set the zone's Look ahead to 0.
  • An error: the message is shown. If it keeps happening, please open an issue with it and the diagnostics file.

A dry run changes nothing and says nothing. A calculation with nothing new to read (every reading was already used) is not a failure. A zone switched to manual or disabled is not calculated, so it shows no such problem.

docs.title: "The calculated duration looks wrong"
docs.text: The diagnostic file shows the current state, not how it was reached. To find out why a particular day watered the way it did, switch on the calculation log in the general settings (turn on the advanced mode first: the switch is there). From then on every calculation appends one line to config/smart_irrigation/calc_log.jsonl with the sensor records and their aggregation, the module intermediates (solar radiation and whether it was measured or estimated, net radiation, ET0) and the resulting water balance, duration and volume, so two days can simply be compared. The most recent records are also included in the diagnostics download (coordinates rounded, entity ids removed), which makes them easy to attach to an issue.

docs.title: Weather services
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation needs weather data to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) and, from it, how long to run each zone. That data can come from a weather service, from your own sensors, or from a mix of both (configured per field in a sensor group).

Four weather services are supported: three online services, and a weather entity of Home Assistant itself.

docs.title: The services at a glance
docs.text:
Service API key Solar radiation Reference ET0 (FAO-56) Cost Open-Meteo (default) None Yes Yes Free OpenWeatherMap Required No No Free tier, then paid Pirate Weather Required No No Free tier, then paid A weather entity in Home Assistant None No No Free

The online services provide temperature, humidity, dew point, pressure, wind and precipitation. A weather entity provides temperature, humidity, pressure and wind, a dew point when its integration has one, and never the rain that fell (see below). The difference that matters for accuracy is solar radiation.

docs.title: Why solar radiation matters
docs.text:
When Smart Irrigation calculates the evapotranspiration itself, it uses the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation, the agronomic reference for reference evapotranspiration. Solar radiation is its dominant term. Two cases:

  • Radiation available: a full Penman-Monteith calculation. Most accurate.
  • No radiation: radiation is estimated from the temperature range (FAO-56 Eq. 50). Still useful, but less precise, especially in cloudy or coastal climates.

You do not configure this. Radiation is used automatically whenever a source provides it, and estimated from temperature otherwise. There is no "estimation method" toggle to get wrong.

docs.title: Open-Meteo: full Penman-Monteith, out of the box
docs.text:
Open-Meteo provides solar radiation (and a ready-made FAO-56 ET0) directly, with no API key. In a sensor group, set the Solar Radiation source to Weather service. That is all: you get a full Penman-Monteith calculation with no extra hardware and no key.

This is why Open-Meteo is the default and the recommended choice for this integration.

docs.title: OpenWeatherMap / Pirate Weather
docs.text:
These services do not provide solar radiation themselves, but you still have two ways to get a full Penman-Monteith with them:

  1. Let Open-Meteo fill it in (easiest). Set the Solar Radiation source to Weather service in your sensor group. Because OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather do not supply radiation, the integration fetches just that field from Open-Meteo (free and keyless) and labels the option "(via Open-Meteo)" so it is clear where the value comes from. The same applies to the reference ET0. No sensor, no key.
  2. Use a dedicated radiation sensor. Add a pyranometer, or any entity that reports irradiance (some weather stations and a few HA integrations expose it), set it as the Solar Radiation source, and declare its unit (for example W/m²). Use this if you prefer a strictly single-source, on-site measurement.

Without either, ET falls back to the temperature-based estimate described above.

docs.title: A weather entity in Home Assistant
docs.text:
If you already have your national weather service in Home Assistant (DWD, Met.no, KNMI, the NWS, ...) or a station of your own with a forecast, choose A weather entity in Home Assistant and pick the entity. No API key, no second provider, and a run is skipped on the forecast you see in Home Assistant.

  • Current values come from the entity's attributes: temperature, humidity, pressure, wind, and the dew point when the entity has one. They are read in the units Home Assistant shows them in and converted for the calculation. The wind is taken as measured at the standard 10 m and brought to 2 m, the pressure as reported at sea level and brought to your elevation, as for the online services.
  • The forecast comes from weather.get_forecasts: the daily forecast, or else the twice-daily or the hourly one, folded into days. The hourly one, when the entity has it, also gives the rain expected in the hours ahead of a run.
  • No rain that fell. A weather entity only forecasts rain, and a forecast never enters the water balance. Give each sensor group a rain sensor under Current precipitation: a gauge, or a sensor that measures rain. Check that it is a measurement: some weather integrations also offer next-hour or nowcast sensors with the same device class, and those are forecasts. The panel does not offer the weather service for the rain with this choice, and a new sensor group starts with no rain source. After switching, the weather service page names the groups that still take their rain from it, and the log says so for each of them.
  • Solar radiation and reference ET0 come from Open-Meteo, as with OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather.
  • One entity per installation, since the weather service is a general setting. A field can still read any sensor of its own.

docs.title: What reads from Open-Meteo, whatever service you pick
docs.text:
Open-Meteo is the default service and also the one Smart Irrigation turns to for the data the others do not publish. With OpenWeatherMap, Pirate Weather or a weather entity, these still come from Open-Meteo, keyless and free:

  • the sun, hour by hour, for the hourly calculation when no radiation sensor is mapped, and the daily radiation and reference ET0;
  • the hours of the days ahead, for a zone whose module looks ahead.

Your own service's rain is never replaced by Open-Meteo's. With Open-Meteo itself, one more use:

  • with Open-Meteo itself and a sensor group that reads every input of the ET from the weather service (temperature, humidity or dew point, wind, pressure, solar radiation), the hourly calculation is priced on Open-Meteo's own hourly history instead of the readings Smart Irrigation took (see the hourly calculation). What feeds the rain doesn't matter, as rain doesn't enter the ET: a rain gauge of your own keeps the history. A group that measures some inputs of the ET (a thermometer of your own, say) takes the history for the inputs it reads from Open-Meteo and keeps its own values for the others.

None of this is a single point of failure. When Open-Meteo cannot be reached, each of these falls back to what Smart Irrigation can do without it: the sun is estimated from the day's temperature range (FAO-56 Eq. 50) or read from your sensor, the rain comes from the readings, a forecast that is not available leaves the zone on the daily equation, and the hourly calculation sums the readings it recorded. A calculation is made, with a little less precision, and the log says what was missing.

docs.title: Skipping the calculation entirely (Open-Meteo's own ET0)
docs.text: Open-Meteo also returns a finished FAO-56 ET0. To use it as it is, set the zone's Evapotranspiration to Provided by a sensor or a service, and the sensor group's Evapotranspiration source to Ready-made ET₀ from the weather service. Open-Meteo computes that ET0 from its own model data, so it does not take your own sensors into account; the calculation by Smart Irrigation with a radiation source does. See modules.

docs.title: Switching service at any time
docs.text: You can change the weather service whenever you like under Weather › Weather service, without reinstalling the integration. The API-key field is hidden for keyless services such as Open-Meteo, and the key is validated against the service before the change is applied. For a weather entity, Save stays disabled until one is picked.

docs.title: Which should I pick?
docs.text:
• Want it to just work, accurately, for free? Use Open-Meteo (the default) and take Solar Radiation from the weather service.
  • Already invested in OpenWeatherMap or Pirate Weather and want full accuracy? Source Solar Radiation from the weather service (filled from Open-Meteo automatically), or add a dedicated radiation sensor.
  • Already have your national weather service in Home Assistant? Choose A weather entity in Home Assistant, and give each sensor group a rain sensor.
  • No radiation source at all? It still works, on a temperature-based estimate, which is good enough for many gardens.
